docs.title: For Teachers
docs.text: Thank you for looking at Gut Check for your students. This page explains what the book is, who it fits, and how to start. You don't need to read all 20 chapters first. Pick a plan from the Teacher Guide, open one chapter, and spend five minutes playing with its MicroSim.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk is a free, open textbook about the gut-brain axis: the two-way communication between the digestive system, the immune system, and the nervous system. It is written for students in grades 9 to 12 who have had about one year of high school biology. No chemistry beyond the basics is needed.

It also works well for:

  • Students who want health or medical careers, because every chapter connects the science to a fictional patient.
  • Teens living with a gut condition such as Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, IBS, or celiac disease, and their friends and families (see For Families).
  • Wellness-curious students who see "heal your gut" posts online. The book's main lesson is how to tell solid science from hype.

docs.title: What is in each chapter
docs.text:
Every chapter follows the same pattern (see How to Use This Book):

  • a short story or question to open it, often about Riya (who has Crohn's disease) or Sam (who has IBS and test anxiety), both fictional
  • an everyday comparison before any technical words
  • the core science in numbered sections
  • Hype Meter cards that grade popular claims as Strong, Moderate, Preliminary, or Hype (how the Hype Meter works)
  • a "How to read a gut-brain claim" box that applies six questions to one real study
  • a MicroSim, a small interactive simulation that runs in the browser, plus a box on what the model leaves out
  • an At the Bedside case, Common Misconceptions, a Your Gut Check practice section, 12 exercises across Bloom's levels, and Key Takeaways
  • a 10-question quiz with explanations on its own page

See the List of Chapters and the List of MicroSims.

docs.title: How to use it in your course
docs.text:
Chapters 1 to 4 build the foundation. Most later chapters can be taught in any order, and each one lists its prerequisites at the top. Full pacing plans (a 2-week unit, a 6-week unit, a semester elective, and single-lesson drop-ins) are in the Teacher Guide.

Course Good starting chapters Why they fit Biology 1, 3, 4, 6, 12 Organ systems working together, microbes as a community, immunity, and genes and disease (celiac disease) Anatomy and physiology 1, 2, 5, 7, 8 The gut wall, the vagus nerve, hormones, the HPA axis and negative feedback, and pain pathways Health 9, 10, 15, 16, 20 Real conditions, food and mood without food-shaming, supplement claims, and media literacy Psychology 7, 11, 13, 18, 19 Stress, mood, research methods (confounders, cohort studies, trials), therapy, and stigma Science or health club See the Club Kit A ready 10-session plan for 45 to 60 minute meetings

docs.title: Free and printable
docs.text:
The book is free to read online, with no login and no ads. It is licensed under Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0. In plain words:

  • You may use it in class, print it, and share it with students for free.
  • You may adapt it (for example, shorten a chapter or translate it) if you share your version under the same license.
  • Give credit: name the book, link to it, and say if you made changes.
  • Don't sell it or use it commercially.

A credit line like this works: Adapted from "Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk" by Aaryav Sharma, licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. See How to Cite for more formats. The Downloads page has a PDF of each chapter and a PDF of the full book, for printing or offline reading.

docs.title: Using the MicroSims
docs.text:
All 20 MicroSims run in a web browser with no install. Each sim page has the sim, a fullscreen button, How to Use steps, a learning objective, an embed code, and a Lesson Plan with timing, a step-by-step activity, and assessment questions.

Embedding a sim in your own page. Copy the code from the "Iframe Embed Code" section of any sim page and paste it into your course page or learning management system, if it accepts iframes. For example, this is the code for the Peristalsis Builder:

<iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/gut-brain-textbook/sims/ch01-peristalsis-builder/main.html" height="522px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

To embed a different sim, change the folder name (for example, ch07-hpa-stress-dial) and use the height listed on that sim's page.

Predict, observe, explain. This routine works with every sim:

  1. Predict. Before touching anything, students write what they think will happen and why.
  2. Observe. Run the sim and record what actually happens.
  3. Explain. Students explain any surprise in one or two sentences using the chapter's terms.

End with the limits. Every sim lesson plan ends by reading the chapter's "What this model leaves out" box. Asking "what does this model get wrong?" is one of the most useful habits the book teaches.

Pairs work better than solo. One student runs the sim while the other predicts and records, then they switch.

docs.title: Quizzes, practice, and assessment
docs.text:
• Quizzes. Each chapter has a 10-question quiz on its own page, for example the Chapter 1 quiz. Answers sit in "Show Answer" boxes, so copy questions into your own form or handout if you want students to answer without peeking (the license allows this with credit).
  • Your Gut Check. Each chapter's practice section has a claim to grade, three short scenarios, and a data-reading question. It works well as homework or a warm-up.
  • Mock exam. Appendix A: Mock Exam has 50 multiple-choice questions covering all 20 chapters (two or three per chapter), with an explanation for each answer and a one-table answer key. Use it as a cumulative review for the end of a unit or course, or pick the questions for the chapters you taught.
  • Capstone. Chapter 20 ends with a student research project template, where each student grades one real health claim.

More assessment ideas and a rubric are in the Teacher Guide.

docs.title: Teacher resources
docs.text: Resource What it is Appendix C: Teacher Guide Pacing plans, a per-chapter table, a Hype Meter classroom activity, assessment ideas, and differentiation notes Appendix D: Club Kit A 10-session club plan, a claim-checking challenge, and a family night Appendix A: Mock Exam 50 multiple-choice questions across all 20 chapters, with explanations and an answer key Appendix E: Pilot Study Kit A small pre/post study of Chapters 1, 5, 10, and 20 for a club or class: ethics and permission steps, a 10-question quiz with an answer key, an anonymous feedback form, and a scoring and results template (no pilot has been run yet) Downloads PDFs of each chapter and of the full book

docs.title: Teaching sensitive topics
docs.text:
This book is about bodies, food, and feelings, so some of it may be personal for your students. In any class, some students may live with a gut condition, some may struggle with eating or body image, and some may be dealing with anxiety, depression, or thoughts of suicide. You may not know who they are.

  • No one should be asked to disclose. Never ask students to share their own or their family's symptoms, diagnoses, diets, or mental health. Keep discussion on the science and the fictional cases (Riya, Sam, and the At the Bedside patients).
  • Avoid food-shaming. Don't label foods or eaters as "good" or "bad," and don't ask students to log or share what they eat. The book treats food as nourishment, culture, and comfort. Chapters 12 and 15 explain why cutting out foods without a medical reason can backfire, and Chapter 15 discusses eating disorder risk. Preview them before class.
  • Give a heads-up. Chapters 7, 8, 11, 13, and 19 cover stress, pain, mental health, autism and ADHD, and stigma. Tell students ahead of time and offer a way to choose another task without explaining why.
  • Bathroom access. Students with gut conditions may need to leave quickly and often. Chapter 19 explains school accommodations such as 504 plans. A quiet, no-questions bathroom policy helps everyone.
  • Share help. In the US, anyone can call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, free and confidential, 24/7, or chat at 988lifeline.org. Remind students that the school counselor is there for them too. Let your counselor know when you plan to teach the mental-health chapters, and follow your school's reporting rules.
  • Language. Follow the book's lead: autism and ADHD are described as neurodevelopmental differences, not diseases to fix, and the book never says gut changes cause or cure them.
  • Not medical advice. If a student asks whether they should try a diet, supplement, or medicine, the answer is always "talk to your doctor." The cases are fictional teaching cases.

docs.title: Standards connections
docs.text:
These are teacher-made connections

The table shows where chapters connect to NGSS high school life science performance expectations. The connections were made by the book's author to help with planning. The book is not reviewed or endorsed by NGSS or Achieve. Each code links to its official page; check your own state or district standards.

Performance expectation (paraphrased) Chapters How it connects HS-LS1-2: Build and use a model of how interacting body systems are organized in levels to carry out functions in a multicellular organism. 1, 2, 4 The gut wall is a clear example of levels: neurons and smooth muscle form the enteric nervous system, which links to the vagus nerve, brainstem, and immune system. The NGSS clarification emphasizes system-level functions such as nutrient uptake and gives smooth muscle working with other tissues in an artery as an example; in the Peristalsis Builder, enteric neurons and smooth muscle work together to push food along, which is a similar gut example. HS-LS1-3: Plan and carry out an investigation that gives evidence that feedback mechanisms keep the body in balance (homeostasis). 7, 4 Chapter 7 shows cortisol's negative feedback in the HPA axis. In the HPA Axis Stress Dial, students change one variable at a time (feedback on or off, acute or chronic stress) and record the result, a simple simulated investigation. The Cytokine Feedback Loop offers a contrast: a loop that can keep itself going. HS-LS2-6: Evaluate claims, evidence, and reasoning that interactions in an ecosystem keep the numbers and types of organisms fairly steady under stable conditions, and that changing conditions can lead to a new ecosystem. 3, 6 The gut microbiome is a community that stays fairly stable and can shift after a disturbance. In the Microbiome Balance sim, students run an antibiotic course and a diet change and judge whether the community recovers. The "evaluate claims" part matches the Hype Meter.

Many chapters also practice NGSS science practices such as analyzing data, using models, and evaluating claims, especially Chapters 13, 15, 16, and 20.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
• Devices. The book works in a browser on phones, tablets, Chromebooks, and laptops. MicroSims resize to fit the screen.
  • Network. The MicroSims load the p5.js library from cdn.jsdelivr.net. If a sim shows a blank area on school devices, ask your IT team whether that site is blocked.
  • Screen readers. Each MicroSim includes a short text description for screen readers. It summarizes the sim rather than announcing every change, so pair students who use screen readers with a partner and use the sim's "About This MicroSim" section alongside it.
  • More notes are in the Teacher Guide.

docs.title: Tell us how it went, or report an error
docs.text: If you use the book with students, the author wants to hear what worked and what you changed. Please don't include student names or other personal information. The Contact page has forms to tell the author you're using the book, suggest an improvement, or report an error.

docs.title: Fine print
docs.text:
• Not medical advice. This book teaches; it does not diagnose or treat. The At the Bedside cases and the people in them are fictional. Anyone with symptoms should talk to a doctor.
  • Independent. The book is not affiliated with or endorsed by any medical society, patient group, or standards organization.

docs.title: Appendix A: Mock Exam
docs.text:
This mock exam has 50 multiple-choice questions that cover all 20 chapters of Gut Check. Plan on about 60 minutes. It works for self-study before a test, for review after you finish the book, or as a class exam that teachers can assign in full or by part.

How to use it:

  • The questions are grouped into five parts that follow the order of the book. Each part covers four chapters.
  • Choose the best answer for each question before you click Show Answer. Many questions ask you to read data, grade a claim with the Hype Meter, or predict what happens next in a pathway, so take your time.
  • Each answer names the chapter it comes from, so you know where to review.
  • The Answer Key at the end lists all 50 answers in one table for quick scoring.

This exam is for learning. It is not medical advice.

docs.title: Part I: Foundations of the Gut-Brain Axis (Chapters 1 to 4)
Question 1
docs.text:
Which nerve network inside the gut wall mainly controls the lining (secretion and local blood flow) rather than gut movement?

  1. The myenteric plexus
  2. The submucosal plexus
  3. The nodose ganglion
  4. The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The submucosal plexus sits just under the lining and mainly works on the mucosa. The myenteric plexus, between the two muscle layers, mainly controls movement. The nodose ganglion and dorsal motor nucleus belong to the vagus pathway, not to the enteric nervous system.

Chapter: Chapter 1: The Brain in Your Belly (and Why That Phrase Is Misleading) Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A researcher places a short piece of animal intestine, with no connection to the brain or spinal cord, in a warm nutrient bath and slips a small soft ball inside. What should she predict?

  1. The wall squeezes behind the ball and relaxes ahead of it, pushing the ball along.
  2. Nothing happens, because every gut movement needs a command from the brain.
  3. The wall twitches at random but cannot move the ball in one direction.
  4. The ball moves only if the vagus nerve is left attached to the piece.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The peristaltic reflex is a local enteric circuit: stretch triggers contraction behind the food and relaxation ahead of it. Scientists have watched isolated intestine do this since 1755. The brain and vagus can adjust gut movement, but they are not required for this reflex.

Chapter: Chapter 1: The Brain in Your Belly (and Why That Phrase Is Misleading) Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Two posts appear in your feed. Post 1: "Your gut has its own nervous system that can run digestive reflexes without your brain." Post 2: "Your gut has more neurons than your brain." Which pair of Hype Meter grades fits the evidence in Chapter 1?

  1. Post 1: Strong. Post 2: Strong.
  2. Post 1: Hype. Post 2: Strong.
  3. Post 1: Moderate. Post 2: Preliminary.
  4. Post 1: Strong. Post 2: Hype.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Isolated gut segments and Hirschsprung disease give strong evidence that the ENS runs reflexes on its own. But the ENS has about 400 to 600 million neurons, while the brain has about 86 billion, well over a hundred times more. So Post 1 is Strong and Post 2 is Hype.

Chapter: Chapter 1: The Brain in Your Belly (and Why That Phrase Is Misleading) Bloom's Level: Evaluate

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Enteroendocrine cells in the gut lining sense nutrients and release hormones that help tell you that you are full. Which pair of hormones does Chapter 2 name as satiety signals?

  1. Cortisol and ACTH
  2. Serotonin and dopamine
  3. CCK and GLP-1
  4. Insulin and melatonin
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Enteroendocrine cells release gut hormones such as CCK and GLP-1, which act as satiety (fullness) signals. Cortisol and ACTH are stress hormones from the HPA axis (Chapter 7). Serotonin and dopamine are neurotransmitters, not the satiety hormones this chapter describes.

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Vagus Highway Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
An influencer measures her heart rate variability (HRV) before and after five minutes of humming. Her HRV goes up, and she posts: "Humming reset my vagus nerve and cured my anxiety!" Which critique is strongest?

  1. HRV cannot change in a few minutes, so her device must be broken.
  2. Humming only works through spinal nerves, so the vagus could not be involved.
  3. HRV is an indirect estimate of vagal activity at the heart, and a brief shift does not show a "reset" or a treatment for an anxiety disorder.
  4. She should have measured stomach acid instead, because the vagus nerve does not affect the heart.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Small lab studies show that tricks like slow breathing or cold on the face can briefly shift heart rate and HRV. HRV is only an indirect estimate of vagal activity at the heart, and no study in this chapter shows these tricks reset the vagus or treat an anxiety disorder. "Reset" has no scientific meaning here, which is why the claim grades as Hype.

Chapter: Chapter 2: The Vagus Highway Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
A newborn cannot digest human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs). Why do these sugars still matter for the baby's gut?

  1. They feed certain beneficial gut bacteria, such as Bifidobacterium, which helps shape the baby's first microbial community.
  2. They are the main fuel for the baby's brain cells.
  3. They kill all bacteria in the baby's gut so the immune system can develop alone.
  4. They are antibodies that replace the baby's own immune system.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. HMOs pass through the baby undigested and act as food for certain helpful bacteria such as Bifidobacterium. That is one way breastfeeding shapes the early microbiome. They are sugars, not antibodies, and they feed microbes rather than wiping them out.

Chapter: Chapter 3: Meet the Microbiome Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A video claims: "Bacterial cells outnumber your human cells 10 to 1, so you are only 10% human." Which response best matches Chapter 3?

  1. The claim is right; modern cell counts confirmed the 10 to 1 ratio.
  2. The claim is backwards; human cells outnumber bacterial cells 10 to 1.
  3. The claim is wrong because bacteria live only in the stomach, not the colon.
  4. The old 10 to 1 figure is wrong; a typical adult has roughly 38 trillion bacterial cells and 30 trillion human cells, about 1.3 to 1.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The 2016 estimate puts a typical adult at about 38 trillion bacterial cells and 30 trillion human cells, roughly 1.3 to 1. The old "10 to 1" number was never well measured and is wrong. Most gut bacteria live in the colon, not the stomach.

Chapter: Chapter 3: Meet the Microbiome Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Most E. coli in a healthy colon are harmless, yet some E. coli cause serious illness. What best explains this?

  1. Harmless E. coli turn dangerous whenever a person eats sugar.
  2. Different strains of the same species share most genes but differ in some, which can change what they do.
  3. Only E. coli in the stomach are harmful; those in the colon are always safe.
  4. Antibiotics turn commensal E. coli into pathogens by changing their species.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A bacterial strain is a genetic variant within a species. Most E. coli strains are commensals, while some strains are pathogens. That is why careful researchers and labels name the strain, not only the species.

Chapter: Chapter 3: Meet the Microbiome Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
What are Peyer's patches?

  1. Scar tissue left behind after a Crohn's flare
  2. Groups of pacemaker cells that set the rhythm of gut muscle
  3. Clusters of gut-associated lymphoid tissue that sample what you swallow
  4. Patches of microglia on the surface of the brain
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Peyer's patches are part of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), the immune tissue that samples material from the gut. Pacemaker cells in the gut are interstitial cells of Cajal (Chapter 1). Microglia are the brain's own immune cells.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Immune System as a Sense Organ Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
In an animal experiment, researchers cut the vagus nerve and then trigger gut inflammation. The animal still shows some sickness behavior. Which explanation fits Chapter 4?

  1. Sickness behavior is caused only by the vagus nerve, so the cut must have been incomplete.
  2. Sickness behavior comes from the gut itself and never involves the brain.
  3. Cytokines cannot reach the brain at all, so the behavior must be faked.
  4. Cytokines can also signal the brain through circumventricular organs, transport across the blood-brain barrier, and relays from barrier cells.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Chapter 4 describes four routes for immune messages to reach the brain: nerves (especially the vagus), circumventricular organs, transport across the blood-brain barrier, and relays from barrier cells. Cutting one route leaves the others. Sickness behavior is a real, brain-driven response, shown experimentally in humans.

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Immune System as a Sense Organ Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 11
docs.text:
A student's report says: "Inflammation is the cause of depression." Which revision best matches the evidence and the Moderate grade in Chapter 4?

  1. Inflammation can contribute to depression in some people, but not every depressed person is inflamed, and depression has many causes.
  2. Inflammation has no connection to mood, so the sentence should be deleted.
  3. Inflammation causes all depression, so anti-inflammatory drugs cure it.
  4. Depression causes inflammation, but inflammation never affects mood.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. People with depression have higher average inflammation markers, and experimental inflammation lowers mood in healthy adults. But not everyone with depression is inflamed, and an anti-TNF drug did not treat depression overall. That mix is why the claim grades Moderate and needs the words "in some people."

Chapter: Chapter 4: The Immune System as a Sense Organ Bloom's Level: Evaluate

docs.title: Part II: Chemistry, Stress, and Pain (Chapters 5 to 8)
Question 12
docs.text:
The gut's enterochromaffin cells and the brain's neurons make serotonin with different versions of an enzyme. Which enzyme do the brain's serotonin neurons use?

  1. TPH1
  2. TPH2
  3. The serotonin transporter (SERT)
  4. Kynurenine
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The brain makes its own serotonin from tryptophan using TPH2. Enterochromaffin cells in the gut use TPH1. SERT clears serotonin after it is released, and kynurenine is a product of the pathway that uses most dietary tryptophan.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Chemical Messengers and the Serotonin Myth Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 13
docs.text:
A blood test shows that most serotonin in the bloodstream is stored inside platelets. A student concludes, "A blood serotonin test tells us how much serotonin is in the brain." What is the main flaw?

  1. Platelets carry serotonin straight into the brain, so the test would overestimate it.
  2. The brain does not use serotonin, so there is nothing to measure.
  3. Blood serotonin comes from the brain, so the test measures only brain levels.
  4. Blood serotonin comes mostly from the gut and cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; the brain makes its own supply.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. More than 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, and much of it is stored in platelets. Gut serotonin does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so the brain makes its own from tryptophan. A blood level therefore says little about brain serotonin.

Chapter: Chapter 5: Chemical Messengers and the Serotonin Myth Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 14
docs.text:
In people, the three main short-chain fatty acids end up in different places. Why does acetate, rather than butyrate, reach most of the body?

  1. Acetate is made in the brain, not the colon.
  2. Butyrate is destroyed by stomach acid before it reaches the colon.
  3. The colon lining takes up most butyrate and the liver takes up most propionate, so acetate is the one that travels on.
  4. Butyrate cannot be made from fiber, only from meat.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In people, colonocytes take up butyrate as fuel and the liver takes up propionate. Acetate, usually the most abundant SCFA, is left to reach the rest of the body. All three are made in the colon when microbes ferment fiber.

Chapter: Chapter 6: Fiber, Fatty Acids, and the Blood-Brain Barrier Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 15
docs.text:
Sam eats a big bowl of beans. Which sequence best predicts what happens to the fiber?

  1. It passes through the small intestine undigested; in the colon (mostly the cecum and ascending colon), bacteria ferment it into gas and short-chain fatty acids.
  2. Stomach enzymes break it into glucose, which is absorbed in the small intestine.
  3. It is absorbed whole in the small intestine and carried to the brain.
  4. Bacteria in the mouth ferment it into butyrate before it is swallowed.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Dietary fiber is the part of plant food that human enzymes cannot digest, so it reaches the colon intact. There, microbes ferment it, mostly in the cecum and ascending colon, producing gas and SCFAs (acetate, propionate, and butyrate).

Chapter: Chapter 6: Fiber, Fatty Acids, and the Blood-Brain Barrier Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 16
docs.text:
Why does Chapter 6 grade "Short-chain fatty acids protect the human blood-brain barrier" as Preliminary rather than Moderate?

  1. Because SCFAs have been proven to harm the blood-brain barrier in large human trials.
  2. Because the barrier findings come from germ-free mice, and the one small human trial (66 men, one week) measured the cortisol response to stress, not the blood-brain barrier.
  3. Because SCFAs are not made by gut bacteria.
  4. Because no animal study has ever looked at SCFAs and the brain.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. In germ-free mice, the barrier is leakier and microglia are immature, and microbes or butyrate partly reverse this. No human study has shown a change in barrier permeability. The only human trial was small, short, and measured something else, so the grade stays Preliminary.

Chapter: Chapter 6: Fiber, Fatty Acids, and the Blood-Brain Barrier Bloom's Level: Evaluate

docs.title: Question 17
docs.text:
Imagine an experimental drug that blocks the receptors CRH acts on in the pituitary gland. If someone taking it faced a stressful event, what would you predict for the HPA axis?

  1. More ACTH and more cortisol, because the pituitary would work harder
  2. No change, because CRH acts only on the colon
  3. Less ACTH release and so a smaller rise in cortisol
  4. Higher CRH from the adrenal glands, which would replace cortisol
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In the HPA axis, CRH from the hypothalamus triggers ACTH from the pituitary, and ACTH triggers cortisol from the adrenal cortex. Blocking the CRH signal at the pituitary would weaken the next two steps. CRH comes from the hypothalamus, not the adrenal glands.

Chapter: Chapter 7: Stress and the Gut Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 18
docs.text:
Small human experiments show that public-speaking stress can make the small intestine more permeable. Which cell type does Chapter 7 link to this effect?

  1. Interstitial cells of Cajal
  2. Enterochromaffin cells
  3. Red blood cells
  4. Mast cells
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Chapter 7 explains that stress makes the small intestine more permeable through mast cells, immune cells that release chemical signals. Mast cells near nerves are also linked to IBS pain. Enterochromaffin cells make serotonin, and interstitial cells of Cajal set gut rhythm.

Chapter: Chapter 7: Stress and the Gut Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 19
docs.text:
After a gut pain signal reaches the thalamus, which cortex areas does Chapter 8 name as helping turn it into a pain experience?

  1. The insula and the anterior cingulate cortex
  2. The primary visual cortex and the cerebellum
  3. The nodose ganglion and the dorsal root ganglion
  4. The hypothalamus and the adrenal cortex
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The pathway runs from nociceptors in the gut wall to the dorsal root ganglion, the dorsal horn, the thalamus, and cortex areas including the insula and anterior cingulate cortex. Ganglia are clusters of nerve cell bodies outside the brain, not cortex areas.

Chapter: Chapter 8: Pain, Sensitivity, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 20
docs.text:
A person has an inflamed internal organ, but she feels the ache in a patch of skin and muscle somewhere else. What best explains this?

  1. The inflammation has spread through the blood to that patch of skin.
  2. Sensory fibers from the organ enter the spinal cord at the same level as fibers from that body surface, so the brain misreads where the signal came from.
  3. The vagus nerve carries all organ pain straight to the skin.
  4. Her pain is imagined, because real organ pain is always felt exactly at the organ.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. This is referred pain. Gut sensory nerves are sparse and share spinal relay neurons with nerves from the body surface, so the brain can place the pain in the wrong spot. Referred pain is real, not imagined.

Chapter: Chapter 8: Pain, Sensitivity, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 21
docs.text:
Months after a gut infection has fully healed, tests show no remaining inflammation, yet Jordan still has high pain sensitivity that has spread to nearby areas. Which description fits best?

  1. Peripheral sensitization, because the gut tissue is still inflamed
  2. Normal nociception, because pain always matches tissue damage
  3. Imagined pain, because the tests are normal
  4. Central sensitization, a real and reversible turning up of pain signals in the spinal cord and brain
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Peripheral sensitization happens at the gut, usually because of ongoing inflammation, which Jordan no longer has. Central sensitization turns up signals in the spinal cord and brain and can outlast the original injury. Chapter 8 stresses that it is real and reversible, and normal tests never mean imaginary pain.

Chapter: Chapter 8: Pain, Sensitivity, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 22
docs.text:
How does a JAK inhibitor differ from an anti-TNF biologic in treating IBD?

  1. A JAK inhibitor is an antibody given by infusion; an anti-TNF is a vitamin.
  2. A JAK inhibitor is a steroid used only as a short-term bridge.
  3. A JAK inhibitor is a small-molecule pill that blocks enzymes inside immune cells that relay signals from many cytokines; an anti-TNF is a biologic that targets one cytokine.
  4. They are the same medicine sold under two names.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib and upadacitinib are pills that block Janus kinase enzymes inside immune cells, affecting signals from many cytokines at once. Anti-TNF medicines are biologic therapies that block one cytokine, TNF. Corticosteroids are the short-term bridge.

Chapter: Chapter 9: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 23
docs.text:
A teen's colonoscopy shows patches of inflammation in the end of the small intestine and in the colon, with normal areas in between. The inflammation goes through the full thickness of the wall, and there is a fistula. Which diagnosis fits best?

  1. Crohn's disease
  2. Ulcerative colitis
  3. Irritable bowel syndrome
  4. Lactose intolerance
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gut, in patches, with transmural inflammation that can cause strictures, fistulas, and abscesses. Ulcerative colitis affects only the colon and rectum, continuously, in the inner layers. IBS and lactose intolerance do not cause visible inflammation.

Chapter: Chapter 9: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 24
docs.text:
Four weeks after starting a new medicine, Riya feels much better, but her fecal calprotectin is still high. What is the best interpretation?

  1. The test must be wrong, because feeling better means the inflammation is gone.
  2. Inflammation may still be present, since symptoms can improve before the lining heals, so mucosal healing is the goal to check.
  3. High calprotectin means she has IBS now instead of IBD.
  4. She should stop her medicine, because she has reached remission.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Fecal calprotectin acts like a smoke detector for gut inflammation. Symptoms can improve before inflammation is gone, which is why the modern goal is mucosal healing. Decisions about medicine are made with the care team, and maintenance treatment usually continues during remission.

Chapter: Chapter 9: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 25
docs.text:
Theo, 19, has had belly pain about 3 days a month (not continuous) for 8 months, linked to changes in his bowel habits. He has no alarm features, and all other requirements of both versions are met. Which statement is correct?

  1. He meets Rome IV but not Rome V.
  2. He meets both Rome IV and Rome V.
  3. He meets Rome V but not Rome IV, because Rome IV requires pain at least 1 day a week.
  4. He meets neither, because IBS requires daily pain.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Rome IV requires pain at least 1 day a week on average. Rome V counts pain or discomfort at least 3 days a month, as long as it is not continuous. That change is one reason Rome V counts more people as having IBS.

Chapter: Chapter 10: IBS and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 26
docs.text:
About what share of people develop IBS in the year after a gut infection, according to Chapter 10?

  1. About 10%
  2. About 50%
  3. About 90%
  4. Almost no one
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. About 10% of people develop post-infection IBS in the year after a gut infection. That makes infection one known trigger, though most people who get a gut infection do not go on to develop IBS.

Chapter: Chapter 10: IBS and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 27
docs.text:
A relative says, "IBS is just anxiety." Which evidence from Chapter 10 best shows this claim is Hype?

  1. IBS trials have a placebo response of about 27%, so IBS is imaginary.
  2. Anxiety symptoms are never seen in people with IBS.
  3. IBS damages the bowel and causes cancer, so it cannot be anxiety.
  4. A 2019 meta-analysis found a diagnosed anxiety disorder in about 23% of people with IBS, so most don't have one, and IBS involves measurable changes in gut sensitivity.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Anxiety and depression symptoms are more common in IBS, but a diagnosed anxiety disorder appears in only about 23%. IBS also involves measurable changes in gut sensitivity and gut-brain signaling. IBS does not damage the bowel or cause cancer, and a placebo response does not mean a condition is imaginary.

Chapter: Chapter 10: IBS and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction Bloom's Level: Evaluate

docs.title: Question 28
docs.text:
Which description of the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline matches Chapter 11?

  1. It is only for adults and must be booked a week ahead.
  2. It is free, confidential, available 24/7, and can be reached by call, text, or chat.
  3. It charges a fee unless a doctor makes a referral.
  4. It is open only during school hours.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Chapter 11 describes 988 as free, confidential, and available 24/7 by call, text, or chat in the US. Getting help is part of good gut care, and reaching out early is a strength, not a failure.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Anxiety, Depression, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 29
docs.text:
In 2016, researchers moved gut microbes from people with major depression into rats or germ-free mice, and the animals showed depression-like behavior. A post says this "proves gut bacteria cause depression in people." Which evaluation is best?

  1. Strong: animal transfer studies are the highest level of evidence.
  2. Hype: the studies were never done.
  3. Preliminary: rodent behavior is not human depression, and human microbiome studies are snapshots that cannot show direction.
  4. Moderate: because the result happened in two species, it is proven in humans.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. These transfer studies show that microbes can change rodent behavior, which is reasonably supported. But depression-like behavior in rodents is not human depression, and human studies only show that people with depression have somewhat different bacteria at one point in time. That is why the human claim grades Preliminary.

Chapter: Chapter 11: Anxiety, Depression, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Evaluate

docs.title: Question 30
docs.text:
Which blood test does Chapter 12 describe as a main first step in testing for celiac disease?

  1. A zonulin test
  2. A fecal calprotectin test
  3. An IgE skin-prick test
  4. A tTG antibody test
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Celiac diagnosis uses a tTG antibody blood test and, for most people, a small bowel biopsy. IgE tests relate to food allergy, calprotectin flags intestinal inflammation, and commercial zonulin tests do not reliably measure zonulin.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Celiac Disease and Food Reactions Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 31
docs.text:
Celiac disease affects about 1 in 100 people worldwide. In a high school of 1,000 students, about how many would you expect to have it?

  1. About 1
  2. About 10
  3. About 100
  4. About 300
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. One in 100 is 1%, and 1% of 1,000 is 10. Many of those students might not know yet, which is one reason testing matters when symptoms suggest celiac disease. Testing should happen before going gluten-free, because the diet can make tests falsely negative.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Celiac Disease and Food Reactions Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 32
docs.text:
Why do some people with celiac disease become lactose intolerant until their small intestine heals?

  1. Damage to the brush border reduces lactase, the enzyme that breaks down milk sugar.
  2. Gluten and lactose are the same molecule.
  3. The gluten-free diet removes all lactase from the body.
  4. Celiac disease creates an IgE allergy to milk protein.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Lactase sits on the brush border formed by microvilli. When celiac disease damages the lining, less lactase is available, so lactose is harder to digest. As the lining heals on a gluten-free diet, this often improves.

Chapter: Chapter 12: Celiac Disease and Food Reactions Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Part IV: Brain Conditions, Food, and Supplements (Chapters 13 to 16)
Question 33
docs.text:
A 2017 study gave microbiota transfer to 18 autistic children with no placebo group. A 2024 trial randomly gave 103 autistic children either a transplant or a placebo. Why is the 2024 trial better at testing whether the treatment works?

  1. It was done in mice, which removes human bias.
  2. It gave every child the treatment, so no one missed out.
  3. It was larger and compared the treatment with a placebo, so improvement from other causes shows up in both groups.
  4. It measured only parent opinions, which are the most accurate measure.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Open-label studies without a comparison group cannot separate a treatment effect from expectation, time, or other care. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial lets both groups improve for those reasons, so any extra benefit can be seen. In 2024, the trial found no significant difference from placebo on its main behavior measure.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Autism, ADHD, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 34
docs.text:
An autistic 10-year-old who speaks few words starts pressing on his belly, sleeping poorly, and getting upset at meals. Based on Chapter 13, what is the best first step?

  1. Treat the behavior as part of autism that needs no medical check.
  2. Start a strict elimination diet found online.
  3. Assume that changing his gut bacteria will change his autism.
  4. Consider that he may be in pain, for example from constipation, and get standard, respectful medical care.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Communication and interoception differences can make gut pain harder to recognize, so behavior changes may be a sign that something hurts. GI symptoms such as constipation are more common in autistic children and deserve standard care. Treating the pain is separate from autism itself, which is not a disease to fix.

Chapter: Chapter 13: Autism, ADHD, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 35
docs.text:
Which two hallmarks does Chapter 14 describe in the brain in Alzheimer's disease?

  1. Lewy bodies and loss of dopamine neurons
  2. Amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles
  3. Villous atrophy and gluten ataxia
  4. Mast cells and leaky tight junctions
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Alzheimer's disease involves amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles. Lewy bodies and loss of dopamine neurons are features of Parkinson's disease. Gut microbe research in Alzheimer's is very early.

Chapter: Chapter 14: Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 36
docs.text:
Human autopsies show Lewy pathology early in the vagus nucleus, constipation can come years before diagnosis, and mice show alpha-synuclein can travel from gut to brain along the vagus nerve. But human vagotomy studies are mixed. Which overall verdict on "Parkinson's starts in the gut" fits Chapter 14?

  1. Moderate, as a hypothesis for some patients, because human evidence is mostly correlation
  2. Strong, because mouse studies prove it for every patient
  3. Hype, because the gut has nothing to do with Parkinson's
  4. Strong, because removing the appendix prevents Parkinson's
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Several lines of evidence point the same way, but human data are mostly correlational, and the gut-first idea may fit only some patients (the gut-first and brain-first subtypes). Appendix removal shows no overall link with Parkinson's in meta-analyses. Moderate as a hypothesis is the honest grade.

Chapter: Chapter 14: Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and the Gut Bloom's Level: Evaluate

docs.title: Question 37
docs.text:
An observational study finds a steady pattern: each extra daily serving of ultra-processed food goes with slightly more depression symptoms. What does this dose-response pattern add?

  1. It proves ultra-processed food causes depression.
  2. It shows the link is pure chance.
  3. It shows depression causes people to eat ultra-processed food.
  4. It makes a causal story more believable, but it is not proof, since a confounder could rise in the same steps.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A dose-response relationship is what you would expect if an exposure really mattered, so it strengthens a causal story. But money, stress, or existing low mood could rise along with the exposure and create the same pattern. Only well-designed trials can test cause directly.

Chapter: Chapter 15: Food and Mood Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 38
docs.text:
In 2024, 13.7% of US households were food insecure. Why does this fact matter for food and mood research?

  1. It shows that food has no effect on mood.
  2. It proves that ultra-processed food causes food insecurity.
  3. Healthy eating is not equally easy for everyone, and money and stress can affect both diet and mood, confounding observational links.
  4. It means diet should replace treatment for depression.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Food insecurity means some families cannot reliably get enough food, let alone choose a particular diet. Money and stress can shape both what people eat and how they feel, so they can create links that look causal. Diet never replaces treatment for depression.

Chapter: Chapter 15: Food and Mood Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 39
docs.text:
What does Chapter 16 say about the word "psychobiotic"?

  1. It is an FDA-approved category of mood medicines.
  2. It is a research term from 2013, not an approved category.
  3. It is a legal term for any probiotic sold in a pharmacy.
  4. It means a probiotic proven to cure depression.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. "Psychobiotic" was coined as a research term in 2013 for microbes that might benefit mental health. It is not an approved category. In the US, most probiotics are dietary supplements, which do not need FDA approval before sale and cannot claim to treat disease.

Chapter: Chapter 16: Probiotics, Prebiotics, and "Psychobiotics" Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 40
docs.text:
Two probiotic products sit on a shelf. Product X has 50 billion CFU of a strain that has never been tested for anything. Product Y has 5 billion CFU of a named strain that was tested in a trial for the condition it targets. Which is better supported, and why?

  1. Product Y, because what matters is the tested strain, at the tested dose, for the tested condition
  2. Product X, because more CFU always means a bigger benefit
  3. Product X, because all probiotics are basically the same
  4. Neither, because CFU counts only dead bacteria
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Probiotic effects are strain specific, and more CFU is not automatically better. The best evidence is for a tested strain at the tested dose for the tested condition, counted at the end of shelf life. CFU counts live microbes, not dead ones.

Chapter: Chapter 16: Probiotics, Prebiotics, and "Psychobiotics" Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 41
docs.text:
A probiotic trial in 30 people measured 12 different outcomes. Its main outcome, chosen in advance, did not change, but one other outcome did. The press release reports only that one. What is the best conclusion?

  1. The probiotic is proven to work, because one result was significant.
  2. The trial was larger than most, so every result is reliable.
  3. With many outcomes measured, one positive result could be chance, and the primary outcome set in advance did not improve.
  4. Primary outcomes do not matter once a trial is published.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A primary outcome set in advance protects against picking whichever result looks good. In a small trial that measured many outcomes, one positive result can easily happen by chance. Chapter 16 says to be wary of exactly this pattern.

Chapter: Chapter 16: Probiotics, Prebiotics, and "Psychobiotics" Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Part V: Treatments, Daily Life, and Reading Claims (Chapters 17 to 20)
Question 42
docs.text:
In July 2025, the FDA approved implanted vagus nerve stimulation for which additional condition?

  1. Crohn's disease
  2. Anxiety
  3. Irritable bowel syndrome
  4. Rheumatoid arthritis
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Implanted VNS is FDA approved for drug-resistant partial-onset epilepsy (1997, add-on), treatment-resistant depression in adults (2005, add-on), as the Vivistim System, arm-movement rehabilitation after stroke (August 27, 2021), and, as the SetPoint System, moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis in adults (July 30, 2025). It is not approved for Crohn's disease, IBS, or anxiety.

Chapter: Chapter 17: Medicine for the Gut-Brain Axis Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 43
docs.text:
A family reads about Vowst and asks whether it is approved to treat their teenager's ulcerative colitis. What is the accurate answer?

  1. Yes, Vowst is approved for any gut disease caused by microbes.
  2. No, Vowst is approved only to prevent recurrent C. diff in adults (18 and older) after antibiotics; FMT for ulcerative colitis remains experimental.
  3. Yes, because FDA approval for one condition covers related conditions.
  4. No, because Vowst has not been approved for anything.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Vowst (April 26, 2023) is approved for one specific use: preventing recurrence of C. diff infection in adults after antibiotic treatment. FDA approval is always for a specific use, so it does not extend to ulcerative colitis. FMT for ulcerative colitis, Crohn's, autism, and Parkinson's remains experimental.

Chapter: Chapter 17: Medicine for the Gut-Brain Axis Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 44
docs.text:
According to Chapter 18, about how many US high school students got 8 hours of sleep on school nights in 2025?

  1. About 1 in 4
  2. About 3 in 4
  3. About 9 in 10
  4. Almost all of them
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Only about 1 in 4 US high school students got 8 hours on school nights in 2025, even though teens need 8 to 10 hours per 24 hours. Puberty also shifts teen sleep timing up to 2 hours later.

Chapter: Chapter 18: Sleep, Exercise, and Therapy Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 45
docs.text:
Light mainly sets the brain's master clock. According to Chapter 18, which cue mainly helps set the rhythm inside the gut?

  1. The phase of the moon
  2. Room temperature
  3. Meal timing
  4. Heart rate variability
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The body has two main timing cues: light, which sets the brain's master clock, and meals, which help set the rhythm inside the gut. Gut microbes also rise and fall on a daily schedule set largely by when you eat.

Chapter: Chapter 18: Sleep, Exercise, and Therapy Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 46
docs.text:
In the 2025 CDC survey described in Chapter 19, what share of US high school students reported persistent sadness or hopelessness?

  1. About 3%
  2. About 10%
  3. About 70%
  4. About 33%
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In 2025, 33.3% of US high school students reported persistent sadness or hopelessness. Stigma is a major barrier to getting mental health help, especially for young people and minority groups.

Chapter: Chapter 19: Culture, Food, Family, and Stigma Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 47
docs.text:
Maya, 15, has Crohn's disease. She needs to use the restroom without asking each time and needs extra time to make up tests she misses during flares. Which school tool is designed for this?

  1. A 504 plan
  2. A permission slip signed each morning
  3. A peer support group
  4. A low-FODMAP diet plan
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A 504 plan is a written plan, made by the school with the student and family, that lists accommodations a student with a disability needs for equal access to education. Peer support is valuable too, but it does not set formal school accommodations.

Chapter: Chapter 19: Culture, Food, Family, and Stigma Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 48
docs.text:
A supplement trial reports a side effect in 2 of 1,000 people on placebo and 4 of 1,000 people on the supplement. A headline says the supplement "doubles your risk." What is the absolute risk difference?

  1. About 50 extra cases per 1,000 people
  2. About 2 extra cases per 1,000 people (0.2 percentage points)
  3. About 200 extra cases per 1,000 people
  4. There is no difference, because both numbers are small
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The relative risk is 4 divided by 2, so "doubles" is technically true. The absolute difference is 4 minus 2, or 2 extra cases per 1,000 people (0.2 percentage points). Only together do the two numbers tell the whole story.

Chapter: Chapter 20: Be Your Own Scientist: Reading Health Claims Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 49
docs.text:
A treatment cuts the chance that an infection comes back from 30% to 10%. What is the number needed to treat (NNT)?

  1. About 2
  2. About 3
  3. About 5
  4. About 20
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The absolute risk difference is 30% minus 10%, or 0.20. The NNT is 1 divided by 0.20, which is 5. So about 5 people need the treatment for one extra person to avoid a recurrence.

Chapter: Chapter 20: Be Your Own Scientist: Reading Health Claims Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 50
docs.text:
A study of a gut supplement was paid for by the company that sells it. According to Chapter 20, how should a careful reader treat this?

  1. Ignore the funding, because peer review removes all bias.
  2. Reject the study automatically, because company-funded studies are always false.
  3. Assume the results are stronger, because companies run the best trials.
  4. Treat it as a reason to look harder at the design and numbers, since industry sponsorship is linked to more favorable results.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A 2017 Cochrane review found that studies sponsored by the maker more often reported favorable results and conclusions. Chapter 20 says this is a reason to look harder, not a reason to dismiss a study automatically. Peer review is a quality check, not a guarantee.

Chapter: Chapter 20: Be Your Own Scientist: Reading Health Claims Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Appendix E: Pilot Study Kit
docs.text:
This kit is for a student or teacher who wants to answer a simple question: do people learn something from reading a few chapters of this book? It is built for a science club, an advisory period, or a class that can spend two or three sessions on the book.

A pilot study is a small, first try at a study. It helps you find problems with your plan and gives you a rough idea of what might happen in a bigger, better-designed study later. It cannot settle the question by itself.

No pilot has been run yet

As of this writing, no pilot study of Gut Check has been carried out, and there are no results to report. If you run one, you will be collecting the first data. Please report what you find honestly, including results that are disappointing.

docs.title: E.1 Purpose and Research Question
docs.text:
Purpose: to check whether students score higher on a short knowledge quiz after reading and exploring selected chapters of Gut Check, and to learn what readers found clear or confusing.

Research question: After reading Chapters 1, 5, 10, and 20 (or a subset of them), do students answer more quiz questions correctly than they did before reading?

Secondary question: How do students rate the chapters for clarity, interest, and usefulness?

What you might expect: average quiz scores will be higher after reading than before. Write your prediction down before you collect any data. Fixing your plan in advance is a small version of preregistration, which you can read about in Chapter 20.

docs.title: E.2 Ethics and Permissions
docs.text:
Studying people, even with a short quiz, comes with responsibilities. Some of your readers may live with a gut condition or a mental health condition, and none of them should feel pressured, judged, or exposed.

Check the rules first. Before you collect any data from students under 18, check your school's rules and your district's rules. Talk to a teacher, club advisor, or principal. Many schools require permission from a parent or guardian before minors take part in any research activity, even an anonymous one. Follow whatever your school requires, and get approval in writing if you can.

If you plan to publish or present results. If you hope to share your results outside the club (in a science fair, a student journal, a conference poster, or online), you may need review by an ethics committee before you start. This might be an Institutional Review Board (IRB), a science fair Scientific Review Committee, or a similar group. Rules differ by school, fair, and journal, so ask early. Getting review after the data are collected is often not allowed.

Ground rules for every pilot:

  • Voluntary. Anyone can choose not to take part, skip any question, or stop at any time, with no effect on grades, club standing, or anything else. Say this out loud at the start.
  • Anonymous. Do not collect names, student ID numbers, email addresses, or anything else that could identify a person. Use random code numbers instead (see Step 1 below).
  • No health information. No one is asked about their own health, diagnoses, symptoms, medicines, or diet. The quiz tests knowledge from the book, and the feedback form asks only about the book. If a participant brings up their own health, thank them and move on without recording it.
  • Not a grade. Quiz scores are never used for any grade.
  • Respectful discussion. If a group discussion happens, remind everyone that people with gut conditions may be in the room, and that conditions like IBS and Crohn's disease are real and not anyone's fault.
  • Store data safely. Keep paper forms in a folder only the study leader can access. When the results are summarized, follow your school's guidance on how long to keep the forms and how to dispose of them.

docs.title: E.3 Procedure
docs.text:
The study uses a single-group pre/post design: the same group takes the same quiz before and after reading.

Step What happens Time 1. Set up Hand out code cards. Explain the study, that it's voluntary and anonymous, and that it isn't graded. 5 min 2. Pre-quiz Everyone takes the 10-question quiz without any help. 10 to 15 min 3. Read and explore Read the chosen chapters and try their MicroSims (see the session plan). 2 to 3 sessions 4. Post-quiz Everyone takes the same quiz again. 10 to 15 min 5. Feedback form Everyone fills out the anonymous feedback form. 5 min

Step 1: code cards. Before the first session, write random three-digit numbers (like 417 or 862) on small cards, one per person. Each participant keeps their card and writes the same code on the pre-quiz, the post-quiz, and the feedback form. This lets you match a person's two quizzes without knowing who they are. Don't make a list linking codes to names.

Session plan (choose one):

Session Two-session version Three-session version 1 Pre-quiz. Chapter 1 and the Peristalsis Builder MicroSim. Chapter 5. Pre-quiz. Chapter 1 and its MicroSim. 2 Chapter 10 and Chapter 20. Post-quiz. Feedback form. Chapter 5 and Chapter 10. 3 Chapter 20. Post-quiz. Feedback form.

Keep the test fair:

  • Don't show anyone the answer key until after the post-quiz.
  • Don't go over the quiz questions during the reading sessions, and don't teach directly to them. Let the chapters do the teaching.
  • Record, for each session, the date, how long it lasted, which sections and MicroSims were used, and how many people attended (a count only, no names).

docs.title: E.4 The Pre/Post Knowledge Quiz
docs.text:
Print this section on its own page. Use the same quiz for the pre-quiz and the post-quiz.

Code number: ______

Circle the best answer. This is not graded. It's fine to guess.

1. About how many neurons does the enteric nervous system (the nerve network in the gut wall) contain?

  • A. About 86 billion
  • B. About 400 to 600 million
  • C. About 38 trillion
  • D. About 5,000

2. When food stretches part of the gut wall, the peristaltic reflex causes:

  • A. The muscle behind the food to contract and the muscle ahead of it to relax
  • B. The whole gut to relax at once
  • C. The brain to send a signal that starts every squeeze
  • D. The muscle ahead of the food to contract so the food stops moving

3. About how much of the body's serotonin is made in the gut?

  • A. About 10%
  • B. About half
  • C. More than 90%
  • D. None; all serotonin is made in the brain

4. Which statement about serotonin made in the gut is correct?

  • A. It travels to the brain and directly improves mood.
  • B. It is made by gut bacteria only.
  • C. It is the main source of the brain's serotonin.
  • D. It does not cross the blood-brain barrier; the brain makes its own serotonin from tryptophan.

5. SSRI medicines for depression sometimes cause nausea or loose stools when someone first starts them. Why?

  • A. SSRIs kill gut bacteria.
  • B. SSRIs block the serotonin transporter in the gut as well as in the brain.
  • C. SSRIs are made from dairy.
  • D. SSRIs stop the gut from making any serotonin.

6. Which statement best describes irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)?

  • A. It is caused by visible damage to the bowel that a colonoscopy can always see.
  • B. It is not a real condition, because tests are often normal.
  • C. It is a type of inflammatory bowel disease, like Crohn's disease.
  • D. It is a disorder of gut-brain interaction: real symptoms caused by changes in gut sensitivity, gut movement, and gut-brain signaling.

7. Which of these is an alarm feature that means a doctor should look for a cause other than IBS?

  • A. Bleeding from the rectum or unplanned weight loss
  • B. Belly pain that gets better after a bowel movement
  • C. Symptoms that get worse during stressful weeks
  • D. Bloating after meals

8. About what share of highly cited animal studies were later confirmed in human randomized trials?

  • A. Almost all of them
  • B. About 9 in 10
  • C. About one in three
  • D. None of them

9. A rare side effect happens to 1 in 10,000 people who don't take a supplement and 2 in 10,000 people who do. A headline says the supplement "doubles your risk." What is the absolute difference?

  • A. 50 extra cases per 100 people
  • B. 2 extra cases per 100 people
  • C. 1 extra case per 10,000 people
  • D. 10,000 extra cases

10. Which phrase could legally appear on a US dietary supplement label without FDA approval (as long as it carries the required disclaimer)?

  • A. "Treats IBS"
  • B. "Supports digestive comfort"
  • C. "Cures anxiety"
  • D. "Relieves depression"

docs.title: Answer key (for the study leader only)
docs.text:
# Answer Where it's taught 1 B Chapter 1, Section 1.5 2 A Chapter 1, Section 1.7 3 C Chapter 5, Section 5.6 4 D Chapter 5, Section 5.7 5 B Chapter 5, Section 5.9 6 D Chapter 10, Section 10.3 7 A Chapter 10, Section 10.6 8 C Chapter 20, Section 20.4 9 C Chapter 20, Section 20.8 10 B Chapter 20, Section 20.10

Short explanations:

  1. The enteric nervous system contains hundreds of millions of neurons, about 400 to 600 million by common estimates, roughly as many as the spinal cord. The brain has about 86 billion, far more.
  2. Stretch triggers contraction behind the food and relaxation ahead of it. This local reflex works without a command from the brain.
  3. More than 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, mostly by enterochromaffin cells (some estimates say about 95%).
  4. Serotonin made in the gut does not cross the blood-brain barrier. The brain makes its own serotonin from tryptophan, an amino acid that can cross.
  5. SSRIs block the serotonin transporter in both the brain and the gut, which is why early stomach side effects are common.
  6. IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction. It is real even though the usual tests are often normal, and it is different from inflammatory bowel disease.
  7. Alarm features such as rectal bleeding, unplanned weight loss, anemia, or certain family history always need further evaluation.
  8. Only about one in three highly cited animal studies were later confirmed in human randomized trials.
  9. Going from 1 to 2 cases per 10,000 doubles the relative risk, but the absolute difference is only 1 extra case per 10,000 people.
  10. "Supports digestive comfort" is a structure-function claim. Claims to treat, cure, or relieve a disease need drug-level approval.

docs.title: E.5 Anonymous Feedback Form
docs.text:
Give this right after the post-quiz.

Code number: ______

Please don't write your name. There are no right or wrong answers. You may skip any question.

Circle one number for each statement. 1 = Strongly disagree, 2 = Disagree, 3 = Neutral, 4 = Agree, 5 = Strongly agree.

# Statement F1 The chapters explained ideas in a way I could understand. 1 2 3 4 5 F2 The everyday comparisons helped me understand the science. 1 2 3 4 5 F3 The MicroSims (interactive simulations) helped me understand how the gut works. 1 2 3 4 5 F4 The Hype Meter helped me think about whether a health claim is believable. 1 2 3 4 5 F5 The chapters kept my interest. 1 2 3 4 5 F6 I feel more confident checking a gut-health claim I see online than I did before. 1 2 3 4 5 F7 I would recommend this book to a friend. 1 2 3 4 5

Q1. What was the most helpful part of these sessions (a chapter, a MicroSim, a case, a Hype Meter card, or something else)? Why?

Q2. What was confusing, or what would you change to make the book better?

docs.title: E.6 Scoring and Summarizing
docs.text:
Score the quizzes. Give 1 point for each correct answer, so each quiz has a score from 0 to 10. Only include people who have both a pre-quiz and a post-quiz with the same code number. Report how many people you had to leave out and why.

For each person, find the change: post-quiz score minus pre-quiz score. A positive number means the score went up.

For the whole group, calculate:

  • Average pre-quiz score: add up all the pre-quiz scores and divide by the number of people.
  • Average post-quiz score: the same, for the post-quiz.
  • Average change: add up everyone's change and divide by the number of people. (This equals the average post-quiz score minus the average pre-quiz score.)
  • Share improving: the number of people whose score went up, divided by the total number of people, as a percentage. Also report how many stayed the same and how many went down.
  • Question by question: for each question, the percentage of people who got it right before and after. This shows which ideas the chapters taught well and which ones need work.

For the feedback form, report the average rating (1 to 5) for each statement, and the number of people who answered it. For the open questions, read all the answers, group similar comments into a few themes, and count how many comments fit each theme. Quote short comments only if they can't identify anyone.

What a pilot like this can and can't show

A small pre/post study without a comparison group can't prove that the book caused any learning. Scores might go up because people saw the same questions twice, because they talked about the topics with friends, because they learned the same ideas in another class, or because they tried harder the second time. The study leader also knows the goal of the study, so it isn't blinded. And a club group is not a random sample of all students. A fair conclusion sounds like: "In this small group, average scores rose from X to Y after reading. A larger study with a comparison group would be needed to know whether the book caused the change." Grade your own result with the Hype Meter: a single small pilot is Preliminary evidence at best.

Ideas for a stronger follow-up study: add a comparison group that reads something else (or the same chapters later), use a different but equally hard version of the quiz for the post-quiz, check whether people remember the ideas a few weeks later, and include more than one school.

docs.title: E.7 Results Template
docs.text:
Copy this table and fill it in. Leave cells blank rather than guessing.

If you run a pilot and want to share what you learned, the author would be glad to hear about it, especially about questions or chapters that confused readers. Never share forms or any information that could identify a participant.

docs.title: Appendix F: Questions to Ask Your Doctor
Appendix F: Questions to Ask Your Doctor
docs.text:
Doctor visits can feel short, and it's easy to forget what you wanted to ask. This page is a list of questions that a teen, a parent, or a guardian might bring to an appointment. It contains questions only, not answers. Your doctor, nurse, dietitian, or pharmacist knows your situation and is the right person to answer them.

Pick the questions that fit you, cross out the rest, and add your own. There are no silly questions.

Printing this page

This page prints cleanly with your browser's Print command (Ctrl+P on Windows, Cmd+P on a Mac). You can also choose "Save as PDF" in the print window to keep a copy on your phone.

docs.title: Before the Visit
docs.text:
Questions to ask yourself (and write down the answers):

  • What symptoms have I noticed? When did each one start?
  • How often do they happen, and how long do they last?
  • Does anything seem to make them better or worse (certain foods, stress, sleep, exercise, time of day)?
  • Have I noticed blood in my stool, weight loss I didn't plan, fevers, or symptoms that wake me up at night?
  • What medicines am I taking, including ones bought without a prescription?
  • What vitamins, supplements, probiotics, or herbal products am I taking?
  • Have I changed my diet recently? What did I change?
  • Does anyone in my family have a gut condition, celiac disease, or colon cancer?
  • What are the top three questions I most want answered today?
  • Who will come with me, and do I want some time to talk with the doctor alone?

docs.title: General Gut Symptoms
docs.text:
• What do you think might be causing my symptoms?
  • What other conditions could cause symptoms like these?
  • Which tests do you recommend, and what will each one tell us?
  • What happens during each test, and how do I get ready for it?
  • When and how will I get the results?
  • Which symptoms mean I should call you right away or go to the emergency room?
  • Should I keep a symptom diary? What should I write in it?
  • When should I come back for a follow-up visit?

docs.title: Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis
docs.text:
• Which type of inflammatory bowel disease do I have, and which parts of my gut does it affect?
  • How active is my disease right now?
  • What is the goal of my treatment (for example, feeling better, or healing the lining of my gut)?
  • What are my treatment options, and what are the benefits and risks of each?
  • How will we know if a treatment is working?
  • What does a flare look like for me, and what should I do if I think one is starting?
  • Which tests will I need to keep track of my disease, and how often?
  • Can IBD affect parts of my body outside the gut, such as my joints, skin, or eyes? What should I watch for?
  • How might IBD affect my growth, energy, or schoolwork?
  • Is it common to feel anxious or down with IBD? Who can I talk to about that?

docs.title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)
docs.text:
• How did you decide that my symptoms are IBS? Which other conditions were ruled out?
  • Which type of IBS do I have?
  • Which symptoms would be a sign that something other than IBS is going on?
  • What treatment options are there for my type of IBS?
  • Would a diet change, such as a low-FODMAP diet, make sense for me? Should a dietitian guide it?
  • Could a therapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy or gut-directed hypnotherapy help me? How would I find someone trained in it?
  • How does stress affect my IBS, and what can I do about it?
  • What should I expect over time? Will my symptoms change?

docs.title: Celiac Disease
docs.text:
• Should I be tested for celiac disease?
  • Should I keep eating gluten until testing is finished?
  • What do my blood test results mean? Do I need a biopsy?
  • If I have celiac disease, can I meet with a dietitian who knows about it?
  • How careful do I need to be about small amounts of gluten?
  • Should my family members be tested?
  • What follow-up tests will I need, and how often?
  • How do I handle meals at school, at friends' houses, and at restaurants?

docs.title: Mood, Stress, and Sleep
docs.text:
• Can my gut symptoms and my mood affect each other?
  • I've been feeling stressed, anxious, or down. Can we talk about that?
  • Is it possible that some of my symptoms are related to stress? How would we know?
  • Who could I see for mental health support, such as a counselor, psychologist, or psychiatrist?
  • Can my medicines affect my mood or my sleep?
  • How much sleep should someone my age get, and could poor sleep be making my symptoms worse?
  • What should I do if I ever feel hopeless or think about hurting myself?

docs.title: Medicines and Side Effects
docs.text:
• What is this medicine for, and how does it work?
  • How and when should I take it? What if I miss a dose?
  • What side effects are common, and which ones are serious?
  • Which side effects mean I should call you right away?
  • How long will it take to know if it's working?
  • Does it interact with my other medicines, supplements, or foods?
  • Will I need blood tests or other checks while I take it?
  • Can it affect my vaccines, my risk of infections, or my ability to play sports?
  • What should I do before I stop taking it or change how I take it?
  • Who should I call if I have questions between visits?

docs.title: Diet and Supplements
docs.text:
• Is this diet safe for me?
  • Is this supplement or probiotic safe for me? Could it interact with my medicines?
  • Is there good evidence that this supplement or diet helps people with my condition?
  • Are there foods I should avoid, or is that different for each person?
  • Am I getting enough nutrients, such as iron, calcium, and vitamin D?
  • Could I meet with a registered dietitian?
  • How can I tell if a change in my diet is actually helping?
  • What should I do if a diet change makes me feel worse or makes eating stressful?

docs.title: School and Activities
docs.text:
• Would a 504 plan or other school accommodations help me? Can you write a letter to support that?
  • What kinds of accommodations do students with my condition often use (bathroom passes, a water bottle, extra time, rest breaks, help with missed work)?
  • Is it safe for me to play sports, run, or do PE? Do I need to change anything?
  • What should I tell coaches, teachers, or the school nurse, and what can I keep private?
  • What should I do if I have symptoms during a test, a game, or a field trip?
  • How should I handle medicines at school or on overnight trips?
  • How can I keep up with schoolwork during a flare or a hospital stay?

docs.title: A Claim I Saw Online
docs.text:
• I saw this post (or video, or ad). Is it true for someone like me?
  • Was this claim tested in people or only in animals or cells?
  • Does this product have FDA approval for my condition, or is it a supplement?
  • Is there any risk in trying it, given my condition and my medicines?
  • Where can I find trustworthy information about my condition?
  • How can I tell if a website or influencer is reliable?
  • Are there clinical trials I could learn about, and how would I know if one is legitimate?

docs.title: My Own Questions
docs.text:
This page is for learning and for planning conversations with your care team. It is not medical advice. Do not start, stop, or change any medicine, diet, or supplement without talking to your doctor.

If you are struggling right now: If you are thinking about suicide or are in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (in the US), or chat at 988lifeline.org. It is free, confidential, and available 24/7. You can also go to the nearest emergency room. Outside the US, you can find a helpline at findahelpline.com.

docs.title: Appendix C: Teacher Guide
docs.text:
This guide helps you plan with Gut Check. It has four pacing options, a one-row-per-chapter teaching table, a Hype Meter activity you can run in any class, assessment ideas, and notes on differentiation and accessibility. For an overview of the book, licensing, and embedding sims, start with For Teachers. Before teaching, read the notes on teaching sensitive topics.

All times assume class periods of about 50 minutes. Every MicroSim page has its own Lesson Plan with timing, steps, and assessment questions, so check it before class.

docs.text:
This fits inside a biology, anatomy, or health course. It covers the foundations, one condition, and the claim-checking skills.
