docs.title: Microbiome Balance
docs.text: Run the Microbiome Balance MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Your colon is home to a crowded community of bacteria, the gut microbiota. A healthy community is diverse, and its normal residents (commensal bacteria) keep potentially harmful opportunists in check, a protection called colonization resistance. Antibiotics save lives, but they also knock down commensals. Human studies show that gut diversity drops quickly during an antibiotic course and that most of the community regrows within weeks, though recovery is not always complete and differs from person to person.

This MicroSim is a cartoon community of 24 made-up species in five groups: fiber fermenters, butyrate producers, Bifidobacteria, other commensals, and opportunists (tomato red). Each group has a few abundant species and several rare ones.

  • The dot field shows the community; each dot is a small share of it.
  • The bar shows each group's share, with percentages.
  • The chart tracks a diversity index (the Shannon index: higher means more kinds of bacteria, more evenly mixed). Antibiotic days are shaded.
  • The panel shows the day, the diversity index, and how many of the 24 species are still present.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press Start and watch the community stay roughly stable.
  2. Predict what an antibiotic course will do to diversity, then press Give antibiotic course. Watch the opportunists bloom while commensals shrink.
  3. Keep the sim running and watch the commensals regrow and push the opportunists back down. When the diversity line levels off, check Species present. Did any species disappear for good?
  4. Press New person and repeat the antibiotic course. Compare how many species this person loses.
  5. Press Reset, then switch the Diet to Low-fiber, high-sugar for a couple of months of simulated time. Watch the makeup and the diversity index, then switch back to fiber-rich.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Apply. The learner will predict how an antibiotic course and a change in diet shift the diversity and makeup of a gut bacterial community, and explain why recovery is often partial and differs between people.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (biology, ecology, or health science)

Duration: 25 to 30 minutes

Activity:

  1. Warm-up (3 minutes). Ask: "If you take an antibiotic, what happens to the bacteria in your gut, and do they come back?" Students write a prediction.
  2. Explore (8 minutes). In pairs, students run one antibiotic course and record the starting diversity index, the lowest value, the value about 100 days later, and the number of species lost.
  3. Compare people (6 minutes). Each pair presses New person twice and repeats the course. The class pools results and discusses why responses differ.
  4. Diet test (5 minutes). Students switch to the low-fiber diet for about 60 simulated days, then back, and describe what changed and whether it reversed.
  5. Limits (3 minutes). Read the "What this model leaves out" box in Chapter 3 and name one way real gut communities differ from the sim.

Assessment questions:

  1. Why do the opportunists bloom during the antibiotic course, and why do they shrink again afterward?
  2. Why doesn't diversity always return to exactly where it started?
  3. Two "people" got the same antibiotic course but lost different numbers of species. What in the sim explains this, and what might explain it in real people?
  4. Why can't this sim predict what an antibiotic will do to your own microbiome?

docs.title: Cytokine Feedback Loop
docs.text: Run the Cytokine Feedback Loop MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
When the gut is inflamed, immune cells release cytokines, chemical messengers such as interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor (TNF). These messages reach the brain through the vagus nerve, through small brain areas without a full blood-brain barrier, and across the barrier itself. The brain, including its immune cells (microglia), responds with sickness behavior: tiredness, poor sleep, low appetite, and low mood.

This MicroSim shows that pathway as a loop of six boxes. Red arrows carry signals forward: gut inflammation to cytokines, cytokines to the brain, and the brain to sleep problems and low mood. Purple arrows carry feedback: in human studies, poor sleep is linked to slightly higher inflammation markers, stress raises some cytokines, and in people with IBD high stress is linked to more symptom flares (an association, not proof of cause). So sleep problems and stress push signal back into the start of the loop, and stress pushes on both the cytokine box and the gut inflammation box. Boxes fill with color and arrows thicken as signals grow, and a meter in the middle shows the overall loop strength.

The link menu lets you break one part of the loop: treat the gut inflammation, protect sleep, or manage stress.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Leave the defaults (gut inflammation 2, sleep 8 hours, stress 3) and press Start. Notice that the loop stays fairly quiet.
  2. Drag Gut inflammation to 8, as in a flare. Watch the cytokine box light up first, then the brain, then sleep problems and low mood. Record the loop strength.
  3. Drop Sleep to 5 hours and raise Life stress to 8. The loop grows stronger even though you didn't change the gut slider. Why?
  4. Use the link menu to choose Treat gut inflammation, then Protect sleep, then Manage stress. Wait for the meter to settle each time and record the loop strength.
  5. Press Reset to return to the starting settings.

docs.title: Serotonin: Where Does It Go?
docs.text: Run the Serotonin: Where Does It Go? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
More than 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, mostly by enterochromaffin (EC) cells in the gut lining. But serotonin made in the gut does not cross the blood-brain barrier. The brain makes its own serotonin from tryptophan, an amino acid from food that can cross.

This MicroSim is a cut-away map of the body, from the gut at the bottom to the brain at the top:

  • Orange EC cells in the gut lining release purple serotonin dots. Each dot acts on the gold nerve under the lining (sending a pulse up the vagus nerve to the brainstem), is pumped back into a lining cell by the serotonin transporter (SERT), or enters the blood, where platelets store it.
  • Serotonin that reaches the blood-brain barrier bounces off.
  • Green tryptophan dots from a protein meal enter the blood. Most turn gray, because most tryptophan is used by other pathways (mainly the kynurenine pathway). A few pass through transporter gates in the barrier and become serotonin inside brain neurons.
  • The SSRI checkbox blocks SERT, the way medicines like fluoxetine do. Watch what happens to gut serotonin, platelets, and brain serotonin.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press Release gut serotonin. Follow the purple dots and watch the counters. Does the "gut serotonin in brain" counter ever rise above zero?
  2. Press it a few more times. Notice the gold pulses traveling up the vagus nerve: that's a nerve signal, not serotonin.
  3. Press Eat protein (tryptophan). Most green dots turn gray. Count how many reach the brain and become serotonin there.
  4. Check SSRI (blocks SERT) and release gut serotonin again. Compare the nerve-signal and platelet counters with step 1.
  5. Press Reset to clear the counters. Uncheck Show labels to quiz yourself on the parts.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Understand. The learner will distinguish gut (peripheral) serotonin from brain (central) serotonin by tracing where gut serotonin goes and explaining how the brain makes its own serotonin from tryptophan.

docs.title: Fiber to Butyrate
docs.text: Run the Fiber to Butyrate MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Your own enzymes can't digest dietary fiber, so it travels to the colon, where gut microbes ferment it. Fermentation makes gas and three main short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): acetate (usually the most abundant), propionate, and butyrate. In people, the colon lining takes up butyrate, the liver takes up much of the propionate, and acetate travels on to the rest of the body.

This MicroSim draws the colon as a tube. Green strands of fiber enter on the left. Colored bacteria ferment them into blue acetate, orange propionate, and red butyrate dots. Butyrate dots move into the row of colonocytes (colon-lining cells), which glow brighter as their fuel rises, while the gaps between cells (the tight junctions) seal more tightly. Three meters track fermentation, colonocyte fuel, and the tight junction seal.

A separate purple panel with a dashed border shows two findings from germ-free mice only: microglia (the brain's immune cells) mature, and the blood-brain barrier tightens, when microbes are present (bars) compared with germ-free mice (black lines). The panel stays fixed when you move the sliders, because those studies compared mice with and without microbes, not different amounts of fiber. These effects have not been shown in people, and the panel can be hidden to make that point.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start at the default (16 grams of fiber a day, about the US average, and medium diversity). Predict which SCFA dots will be most common. Press Start.
  2. Watch which dots move into the colon wall. Notice that only butyrate does.
  3. Drag Fiber to 0, then to 30 grams a day. Watch the three meters and the color of the colonocytes.
  4. Set fiber to 25 grams and drag Diversity from very low to very high. Compare the colonocyte fuel meter.
  5. Uncheck Show mouse-only panel. Notice that nothing in the human part of the model changes, and read the message that replaces the panel.
  6. Press Reset to return to the starting settings.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Understand. The learner will trace dietary fiber through bacterial fermentation to acetate, propionate, and butyrate and their effects on colonocytes and tight junctions, and distinguish these from brain effects shown only in germ-free mice.

docs.title: HPA Axis Stress Dial
docs.text: Run the HPA Axis Stress Dial MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
When you face a stressor, your hypothalamus releases CRH, which tells the pituitary gland to release ACTH, which tells the adrenal glands to release cortisol. This chain is the HPA axis. Cortisol then acts back on the hypothalamus and pituitary to turn CRH and ACTH down. That negative feedback is the stress system's off switch.

This MicroSim shows the three glands as linked boxes that turn from green to red as their hormone rises, with a dashed blue arrow for negative feedback. A gut panel shows three effects of stress signaling: colon movement (CRH speeds up the colon), gut sensitivity, and gut permeability (both driven by mast cell activation and CRH in the model, not by cortisol directly). A graph plots CRH, ACTH, and cortisol over 96 illustrative hours, with the stressor shaded.

You can choose one stressful event (acute), a 2-hour stressor like a big exam, or stress every day (chronic), 12 stressful hours each day. You can also switch cortisol feedback off to see what the off switch does.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Leave the settings at their defaults (stress level 6, one stressful event, feedback on). Predict which hormone rises first. Press Start.
  2. Watch the order in the graph: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol. Watch the colon wiggle faster while the stressor is on, and notice how the levels fall back after it ends.
  3. Uncheck Cortisol feedback on and press Start again when the run ends. Compare the peak and the recovery time.
  4. Turn feedback back on and choose Stress every day (chronic). Watch the low points between stressful days and the gut sensitivity meter.
  5. Try stress levels of 3 and 9 with each pattern.
  6. Press Reset to return to the starting settings.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Understand. The learner will explain how cortisol's negative feedback returns the HPA axis to baseline after acute stress but not during repeated (chronic) stress, and describe the gut changes that accompany stress signaling.

  4. Acute versus chronic (6 minutes). Students run the chronic pattern and describe what happens to the low points and to gut sensitivity across days.

docs.title: Pain Amplifier
docs.text: Run the Pain Amplifier MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Pain is not a simple readout of what is happening in the gut. A stretch of the gut wall is picked up by sensory nerve endings, passes through a dorsal root ganglion, enters the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, and travels up to the thalamus and on to brain areas such as the insula and anterior cingulate cortex. Along the way, the signal can be turned up or down.

This MicroSim lets you hold the gut stretch steady and change three "dials":

  • Peripheral sensitivity: how strongly the nerve endings in the gut respond, for example when the gut is inflamed (peripheral sensitization).
  • Central gain: how much the dorsal horn boosts the incoming signal (central sensitization).
  • Brain state: descending signals from the brain that turn spinal pain signals down (calm) or up (stressed).

The meter on the right shows felt pain on a 0 to 10 scale. A navy marker shows what a "typical body" (all dials at their starting values) would feel from the same stretch. All numbers are made-up teaching values.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press Start to watch signal dots travel from the gut to the brain. Leave the gut stretch at 6 and note the felt pain.
  2. Drag Gut stretch down to 3. The signal still travels, but it stays below the pain threshold: the stretch is sensed, not felt as pain.
  3. Set the stretch back to 6. Raise Peripheral sensitivity to 2x. Compare the felt pain with the navy "typical body" marker.
  4. Reset. Now raise only Central gain to 2x. Does it matter whether the boost happens in the gut or in the spinal cord?
  5. With central gain still raised, move Brain state to "very calm," then to "very stressed." Watch the descending line change color.
  6. Find two different dial settings that give the same felt pain. What does that tell you about guessing a cause from a pain score?

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Understand and Analyze. The learner will explain how peripheral sensitization, central sensitization, and descending modulation can change the pain felt from the same gut stimulus, and analyze why a pain score alone cannot reveal where the signal was amplified.

docs.title: IBD Flare Timeline
docs.text: Run the IBD Flare Timeline MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has ups and downs. A flare is a time when the disease is active and causes symptoms; remission is a time when symptoms fade. This MicroSim follows one fictional teen with Crohn's disease for 12 months after diagnosis and draws four curves on the same chart:

  • Gut inflammation (red): how active the immune attack in the gut wall is.
  • Symptoms (orange): belly pain, diarrhea, and urgency.
  • Energy (blue): how much energy the teen has for school, music, and friends.
  • Mood (purple): higher means a better mood.

You can add five kinds of events at any month: Start steroids (S), Start biologic (B), Missed biologic doses (M), Gut infection (I), and Stressful exam week (X). Each event changes the curves in its own way. Steroids calm symptoms within days but are only a short-term bridge. A biologic builds up over weeks and keeps inflammation down. Missed doses let the medicine fade, and inflammation creeps back weeks later. An infection raises inflammation and symptoms for a few weeks. Exam stress raises symptoms and lowers mood, but the model does not let it change inflammation, because the evidence that stress drives gut inflammation in people is unclear.

The green band is a "healing zone," where inflammation is low enough for the gut lining to heal. This is an illustrative teaching model on a 0 to 100 scale. It is not a prediction for any real person.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the starting plan: steroids just after diagnosis (S), then a biologic at month 1 (B). Predict which curve will drop first. Press Start to move the black playhead through the year and read the values in the panel.
  2. Compare the orange symptom curve with the red inflammation curve in the first two months. Which one falls faster, and why might that matter?
  3. Choose Missed biologic doses in the Event menu, set the Month slider to 6, and press Add event. Notice how long it takes for inflammation to climb and how energy and mood follow.
  4. Add a Stressful exam week at month 10. Which curves change, and which one does not?
  5. Press Clear events to see a year with no treatment at all. Then add only a biologic and compare.
  6. Press Reset to return to the starting plan.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Analyze. The learner will relate gut inflammation, symptoms, energy, and mood over time in IBD, and analyze how treatment events (steroids, a biologic, missed doses) and other events (an infection, a stressful week) change each curve differently.

  4. Discuss (6 minutes). Why does inflammation return weeks after doses are missed, not the same day? Why might someone feel fine while inflammation is still present? Connect to mucosal healing and to why doctors keep treatment going in remission.

docs.title: Rome Criteria Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Rome Criteria Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

For learning only

This MicroSim is an educational exercise. It cannot diagnose irritable bowel syndrome or any other condition. Only a clinician, using a full history, an exam, and sometimes tests, can make a diagnosis. If you have symptoms, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is diagnosed mainly from a pattern of symptoms, using criteria written by the Rome Foundation, an international group of experts. This MicroSim turns those criteria into a checklist you can experiment with.

You can choose three versions:

  • Rome IV, adults (2016): recurrent belly pain on average at least 1 day a week in the last 3 months, linked to two or more of three features (related to bowel movements, a change in how often stool happens, a change in how stool looks), with symptoms that started at least 6 months ago. Most published IBS research, including the prevalence numbers in Chapter 10, used this version.
  • Rome V, adults (2026, current): recurrent, but not continuous, pain or discomfort on average at least 3 days a month in the last 3 months, with the same three features and the same timing rule.
  • Rome IV, children and teens aged 4 to 18: belly pain at least 4 days a month over at least 2 months, linked to one or more of the three features, when another medical condition can't fully explain the symptoms.

Fictional profiles cover several cases: Sam (from this book), someone with mild pain only 3 days a month, someone with constant pain, someone whose symptoms started recently, and someone with blood in the stool. The Alarm menu adds warning signs, such as blood in the stool or unplanned weight loss, that always call for medical evaluation, whatever the checklist says. On wider screens, a panel at the bottom compares the same profile across all three versions.

The sim simplifies "at least 1 day a week on average" to "about 4 or more days a month."

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with Rome IV, adults and the Sam profile. Check each green mark against the criteria above.
  2. Choose the Dana profile (pain only 3 days a month). Predict whether she meets Rome IV, then switch the version to Rome V. What changed?
  3. Choose the Marcus profile (pain all day, every day). Compare Rome IV and Rome V. Why does Rome V treat constant pain differently?
  4. Choose the Leah profile. Which rule does she miss? Drag Months since start until she meets the criteria.
  5. Choose the Omar profile. He meets the symptom criteria, but read the alarm message. Why isn't the checklist enough?
  6. Make your own profile with the checkboxes and sliders, and find the smallest number of pain days that meets each version.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Apply. The learner will apply the symptom-based Rome criteria for IBS to fictional symptom profiles, compare how Rome IV (2016), Rome V (2026), and the child and teen criteria classify the same profile, and recognize that alarm features require medical evaluation regardless of the checklist.

  2. Explore (8 minutes). In pairs, students run steps 1 to 4 of How to Use and fill in a table: profile, Rome IV result, Rome V result.
  3. Discuss (6 minutes). Why might Rome V classify more people as having IBS than Rome IV? Connect to the 2026 UK survey in Chapter 10, where 59.0% of people with self-reported IBS met Rome IV and 70.0% met Rome V.
  4. Alarm features (5 minutes). Run the Omar profile. Discuss why a positive diagnosis strategy still includes checking for alarm features.
  5. Limits (3 minutes). Read the "What this model leaves out" box in the chapter and the banner at the top of the sim. Why can't a checklist diagnose anyone?

Assessment questions:

  1. List the three bowel-related features in the Rome criteria for IBS.
  2. A 25-year-old has pain 3 days a month for a year, linked to bowel movements and to looser stools. Does she meet Rome IV? Rome V? Explain.
  3. Why do research numbers like "6.1% of US adults" need the phrase "by Rome IV criteria" next to them?
  4. Name two alarm features, and explain why they lead to more evaluation even when the symptom criteria are met.

docs.title: The Two-Way Street
docs.text: Run The Two-Way Street MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
People with gut conditions such as IBD and IBS report more anxiety and depression symptoms than other people. But a link between two things doesn't tell you which one causes the other. Gut symptoms could worsen mood (gut to brain), mood could worsen gut symptoms (brain to gut), both could happen, or a third factor, such as poor sleep or a hard life event, could worsen both.

This MicroSim follows a simulated cohort of 500 fictional people. Each dot is one person, placed by their gut-symptom score (left to right) and mood-symptom score (bottom to top). Three sliders set the hidden rules: how strongly gut symptoms change later mood, how strongly mood changes later gut symptoms, and how strongly a shared third factor affects both.

The bars compare two ways of studying the cohort:

  • One snapshot: the correlation between gut and mood symptoms measured at the same moment (like a cross-sectional survey).
  • Following people over time: the correlation between earlier gut symptoms and later mood, and between earlier mood and later gut symptoms (like a cohort study).

All numbers are made up for teaching. The sim is not data from any real study.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with the default settings (gut to brain 0.30, brain to gut 0). Note the snapshot correlation and the two "earlier, later" bars.
  2. Now set gut to brain to 0 and brain to gut to 0.30. Compare the snapshot bar with step 1. Can a single snapshot tell you which direction is at work?
  3. Look at the two "earlier, later" bars. Which one is longer now? What does that tell you?
  4. Set both directions to 0.15. What happens to the snapshot and to the two time bars?
  5. Set both directions to 0 and the shared third factor to 0.30. Is there still a correlation? Can following people over time tell you the direction this time?
  6. Press Start to watch the cohort change over time, and New cohort to repeat the experiment with a different group of fictional people.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Analyze. The learner will explain why a gut-to-brain effect, a brain-to-gut effect, and a shared confounding variable can each produce a similar correlation at one time point, and analyze how following people over time helps separate the direction of effects (reverse causation) but cannot by itself rule out confounding.

  3. Analyze (7 minutes). Students run steps 4 and 5 and answer: Which study design (snapshot or following over time) could tell these settings apart? Which setting fools both designs?

  2. What is reverse causation, and how does following people over time help detect it?
  3. Why can a shared third factor fool even a study that follows people over time?
  4. If a real study finds that gut problems predict later anxiety and anxiety predicts later gut problems, what does that suggest?

docs.title: Villi Explorer
docs.text: Run the Villi Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The small intestine is lined with intestinal villi, tiny finger-like projections covered in even tinier microvilli. Together they give the intestine a huge surface for absorbing nutrients. In celiac disease, eating gluten (a protein in wheat, barley, and rye) sets off an immune reaction in the lining. Over time the villi shorten and flatten, a change called villous atrophy, and the intestine absorbs less.

This MicroSim shows a magnified strip of lining. You choose whether the person has celiac disease and whether they eat gluten, then watch the months go by:

  • Has celiac disease + Eats gluten: purple immune cells crowd in, tTG antibodies rise, the villi shrink, and absorption drops.
  • Has celiac disease + Gluten-free diet: symptoms settle within weeks, antibodies fall over months, and the villi grow back slowly.
  • Does not have celiac disease: the villi stay tall on either diet, because gluten doesn't trigger an immune attack.

The Run tests button reports a tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibody blood test and a small bowel biopsy result for the current moment. Running the tests after switching to a gluten-free diet shows why doctors test first.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Keep Has celiac disease and Eats gluten. Predict what will happen to the villi, then press Start.
  2. After several simulated months, press Run tests. Read the blood test and biopsy results.
  3. Switch the diet to Gluten-free diet. Compare how fast the Symptoms meter falls with how fast Villus height recovers.
  4. Press Reset. Let the villi shrink again, switch to gluten-free, wait about a year and a half of simulated time, and then press Run tests. What changed?
  5. Choose Does not have celiac disease and try both diets.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Understand. The learner will explain how gluten exposure in celiac disease causes villous atrophy and reduces absorption, why villi stay normal in people without celiac disease, and why testing must happen before starting a gluten-free diet.

  3. The testing trap (6 minutes). Students run step 4 and explain in one sentence why the tests changed.
  4. Control comparison (4 minutes). Students run step 5 and explain why the person without celiac disease is the "control" in this model.

  2. Why do symptoms improve faster than the villi heal on a gluten-free diet?
  3. Why can starting a gluten-free diet before testing make celiac disease harder to diagnose?
  4. Why do the villi stay normal in the person without celiac disease, even when they eat gluten?

docs.title: Confounder Detective
docs.text: Run the Confounder Detective MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Many small studies have reported that autistic children have different gut microbiomes from non-autistic children. Does that mean autism and the microbiome are directly linked? Not necessarily. A confounder is a third factor that affects both things being compared. In 2021, a large study (Yap and colleagues, Cell) found that differences in diet, often linked to selective eating, explained most of the microbiome differences; direct links with autism were negligible.

This MicroSim lets you investigate the same logic with simulated data. Two groups of 40 children (an autistic group and a comparison group) have different average microbiome diversity scores. Each child also has three hidden variables: diet variety (how many kinds of food they eat), age, and recent antibiotics. You can:

  • Color the dots by each hidden variable to look for patterns.
  • Account for variables with a statistical adjustment and watch what happens to the gap.
  • Draw a new sample to see how much the results change by chance.

The model was built so that group membership has no direct effect on the score. Your job is to discover which variable creates the gap.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the two black average lines. Note the gap shown in the results panel.
  2. Set Color dots by to Age, then Recent antibiotics. Do the colors explain which dots are low?
  3. Set Color dots by to Diet variety. Where are the orange (few kinds of food) dots?
  4. Check Age under Account for, then uncheck it and check Antibiotics. How much does the gap change?
  5. Check Diet variety. What happens to the gap?
  6. Press New sample several times with diet accounted for. Describe the leftover gap.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Analyze. The learner will identify how a confounding variable (diet variety) can create an apparent microbiome difference between an autistic group and a comparison group, and distinguish a confounder from variables that are balanced between groups.

  2. Detect (8 minutes). In pairs, students follow steps 1 to 3 and write down which variable seems to line up with the low scores.
  3. Test (6 minutes). Students follow steps 4 and 5 and record the gap for each choice in a table.
  4. Chance (3 minutes). Students follow step 6 and explain why the leftover gap isn't exactly zero.
  5. Connect (5 minutes). Read Section 13.5 of Chapter 13 and discuss why a confounder doesn't mean the original difference was "fake," only that it has a different explanation. Read the "What this model leaves out" box.

Assessment questions:

  1. What makes diet variety a confounder in this model, while age is not?
  2. Why does the gap shrink when diet variety is accounted for?
  3. Why does the leftover gap change slightly with each new sample?
  4. Why can't statistical adjustment fix a confounder that researchers never measured?

docs.title: Gut-First or Brain-First?
docs.text: Run the Gut-First or Brain-First? MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This is a model of competing ideas, not a proven map of Parkinson's disease. In Parkinson's, a protein called alpha-synuclein misfolds and clumps inside neurons, and the clumping may spread from one neuron to connected neurons (prion-like spread). Scientists disagree about where the first clumps form.

  • The gut-first (body-first) idea says the process can start in the gut wall, climb the vagus nerve to the brainstem, and reach the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra later. It predicts constipation and acting out dreams years before movement symptoms.
  • The brain-first idea says the process starts inside the brain and reaches the dopamine neurons early. It predicts movement symptoms first, with gut problems later.

The body diagram colors each region as pathology builds up there, and red lines show the path the spread takes. The timeline below shows when each symptom appears. The dashed red line marks diagnosis, when movement symptoms begin. All years are made-up "model years" chosen to show the order of events.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Leave the starting point on Gut-first and press Start. Watch the spread climb the vagus nerve.
  2. When the run ends, read the status line: how many model years before diagnosis did constipation begin?
  3. Switch to Brain-first and run it again. Which symptom comes first now? When does constipation appear?
  4. Check Cut the vagus nerve and run both routes. In which route does cutting the nerve change what happens in the brain?
  5. Use Speed to slow the run down, and Reset to return to the starting settings.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Analyze and Evaluate. The learner will compare the gut-first and brain-first hypotheses of Parkinson's disease by the order of early symptoms each predicts, and explain why cutting the vagus nerve matters only in the gut-first route.

Duration: 25 to 30 minutes

  2. Explore (8 minutes). In pairs, students run both routes and record the model year when constipation, acting out dreams, smell loss, and movement symptoms begin.
  3. Test a prediction (6 minutes). Before checking "Cut the vagus nerve," each pair predicts what will happen in each route. Then they test it and compare with the 2019 mouse study and the mixed human vagotomy studies in Chapter 14.
  4. Debate (6 minutes). Half the class argues for gut-first and half for brain-first, using only evidence from the chapter. Then everyone names one piece of evidence that would settle the question.
  5. Limits (3 minutes). Read the "What this model leaves out" box and name one way the model oversimplifies real Parkinson's.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which early symptoms does the gut-first hypothesis predict before diagnosis, and why?
  2. Why does cutting the vagus nerve block the spread in the gut-first route but not change the brain-first route?
  3. A person had constipation for 12 years before a Parkinson's diagnosis. Does that prove their disease started in the gut? Explain.
  4. Name one kind of human study that could help decide between the two hypotheses.

docs.title: Diet Pattern Explorer
docs.text: Run the Diet Pattern Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Headlines often say a food is "linked to" mood. This MicroSim shows why a link is not the same as a cause. It creates 200 simulated people, each with a diet quality score and a low-mood score (higher means more symptoms). All the numbers are made up.

You control two things real scientists never know for sure:

  • The true effect of diet on mood, from none to strong.
  • Which hidden factors exist: food access (money and nearby stores), sleep, and earlier low mood that changes what people eat (reverse causation).

In an observational study, people's diets come from their own lives, so hidden factors can push diet and mood together. In a randomized trial, a coin flip decides who gets diet coaching, which spreads the hidden factors evenly between the groups.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start in Observational study with the true effect at none and all three hidden factors checked. Read the correlation r. Is there a link?
  2. Uncheck the hidden factors one at a time. Watch the correlation shrink. Which factor creates the strongest fake link?
  3. Check them all again and switch to Randomized trial. Compare the two groups' average low-mood scores.
  4. Raise the True effect of diet slider. How does each design respond?
  5. Press New sample several times in trial mode. Notice how much the difference wobbles by chance.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Analyze. The learner will distinguish association from causation in nutrition research by showing that hidden factors can create a diet-mood correlation even when diet has no true effect, and that random assignment removes that confounding.

  2. Explore (8 minutes). In pairs, students follow steps 1 and 2 of How to Use and record the correlation with each hidden factor on by itself.
  3. Compare designs (7 minutes). Students switch to the randomized trial with the true effect at none, then at medium, and record the group difference each time, pressing New sample three times for each setting.
  4. Discuss (6 minutes). Why does the coin flip remove the fake link? Why does the trial's answer still wobble? Connect to the SMILES trial in Chapter 15, which had only 56 people with complete data.
  5. Limits (3 minutes). Read the "What this model leaves out" box and name one way real diet trials are messier than the sim.

Assessment questions:

  1. With the true effect at none, why does observational mode still show a correlation?
  2. What does "Low mood changes eating" represent, and which direction does its arrow point?
  3. Why does random assignment balance hidden factors even when researchers don't measure them?
  4. Why might a small trial give a misleading answer even though it is randomized?

docs.title: Probiotic Trial Reader
docs.text: Run the Probiotic Trial Reader MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Supplement ads love to quote "a clinical study." But one study can be misleading, especially a small one. This MicroSim imagines a made-up probiotic with a small true effect (an effect size of 0.2, shown by the dashed green line). Each time you run a trial, the sim adds random chance, the way real trials do, and plots the result the trial would report as one dot.

You control three parts of the trial design:

  • People per group: small trials scatter widely; big trials land close to the truth.
  • Outcomes measured: each trial reports its best-looking outcome, the way an ad might. Measuring more outcomes makes chance "wins" more likely, which is why good trials name one primary outcome in advance.
  • Placebo group: without a comparison group, the improvement people show just from taking something (the placebo response) gets counted as if the probiotic caused it.

Orange dots are results that would look "impressive" (statistically significant) in a headline.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the 20 example trials (30 people per group, 1 outcome, placebo group on). Notice how widely the dots scatter around the true effect.
  2. Press Run 20 a few more times. Watch the share of "impressive" results and the average reported effect.
  3. Press Clear, set People per group to 300, and run 20 trials. Predict first: will the dots spread out or bunch up?
  4. Press Clear, set people per group back to 30, and set Outcomes measured to 10. Run 20 trials and compare the average reported effect with the true effect.
  5. Press Clear, uncheck Placebo group, and run 20 trials. What happens to the reported effect?
  6. Decide which settings look most like a typical supplement study, and which look like a trial you would trust.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Evaluate. The learner will judge how trial size, the number of outcomes measured, and the presence of a placebo group change how much confidence a reported probiotic result deserves.

  2. Explore size (8 minutes). In pairs, students run 20 trials at 20, 60, and 300 people per group and record the share of "impressive" results and the average reported effect.
  3. Explore outcomes and placebo (8 minutes). Students repeat at 30 people per group with 1, 5, and 10 outcomes, then with the placebo group off.
  4. Discuss (6 minutes). Why does reporting the best of many outcomes inflate results? Connect this to the Rahmannia 2024 review in Chapter 16, where one of four depression scales showed a benefit.
  5. Limits (3 minutes). Read the "What this model leaves out" box in the chapter and name one way real trials differ from the sim.

Assessment questions:

  1. Why do small trials sometimes report large effects even when the true effect is small?
  2. How does naming a primary outcome in advance protect against chance findings?
  3. What does a placebo group add to a trial, and what goes wrong without one?
  4. A supplement ad cites one trial of 20 people that measured 8 outcomes. How confident should you be in its "best" result, and why?

docs.title: Treatment Evidence Map
docs.text: Run the Treatment Evidence Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Headlines often blur the line between a treatment that is FDA approved, one that is still being tested, and one that is just being sold. This MicroSim gives you 13 treatment cards from Chapter 17, one at a time, and three bins:

  • Approved, cleared, or standard care: FDA approved, cleared, or authorized for that exact use, or recommended by guidelines and backed by trials.
  • Experimental (still being tested): studied in people, but the evidence isn't strong enough for approval or routine use.
  • Unproven or unsafe: no good evidence for the claim, or known to carry serious risk.

After each choice, a feedback panel tells you whether you were right and gives a one-sentence reason drawn from the chapter's sources. The same technology can land in different bins: vagus nerve stimulation is approved for epilepsy, depression, arm-movement rehabilitation after stroke, and rheumatoid arthritis, but experimental for Crohn's disease. Statuses are for the United States as of October 2026.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the treatment card at the top. Decide which bin it belongs in.
  2. Drag the card into a bin, or tap the bin.
  3. Read the feedback panel. If you got it wrong, find the word on the card that changes the answer (the condition, the type of device, or the type of evidence).
  4. Press Next card to continue. Your sorted cards appear in each bin with a check or a cross.
  5. When all 13 are sorted, note your score. Press Start over to reshuffle and try again.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Evaluate. The learner will classify gut-brain treatments by FDA status and strength of evidence (approved, cleared, or standard care; experimental; unproven or unsafe) and justify each choice with evidence.

  3. Investigate (7 minutes). Each pair picks two missed cards and finds the matching section of Chapter 17 to explain the correct bin in their own words.
  4. Discuss (6 minutes). Why do the vagus nerve cards land in different bins? Why is a low-dose antidepressant for IBS in the "standard care" bin even though it's off-label?
  5. Limits (3 minutes). Read the "What this model leaves out" box and name one way real evidence is more complicated than three bins.

Assessment questions:

  1. What is the difference between FDA approval, clearance, and authorization for a device?
  2. Why is FMT in different bins for recurrent C. difficile infection and for autism?
  3. What would need to happen for vagus nerve stimulation for Crohn's disease to move into the approved bin?
  4. Why is a do-it-yourself fecal transplant classified as unsafe?

docs.title: Gut and Sleep Diary
docs.text: Run the Gut and Sleep Diary MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Many people with IBS or inflammatory bowel disease notice that their gut feels worse after a bad night. Keeping a diary, which scientists call self-monitoring, can help you spot patterns and give your care team useful information. But a diary can also fool you.

This MicroSim is a one-week diary for three things: hours of sleep, a stress rating (0 to 10), and a gut symptom rating (0 to 10). It opens with sample data, a made-up week for Sam, a fictional student with IBS from the textbook. The top chart shows sleep as blue bars and gut symptoms as an orange line. The scatter plot below compares sleep with gut symptoms for each day, and the panel reports the correlation coefficient r, a number from -1 to 1 that describes how closely two things move together.

The panel always warns you about the small sample (only up to 7 days), and it shows a confounder alert when stress rises and falls with both sleep and gut symptoms, because stress could be the real driver of both.

Privacy: everything you enter stays in this page's memory. Nothing is saved to your device or sent anywhere, and reloading the page erases it.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Look at the sample week. Which day had the least sleep, and what happened to the gut score that day?
  2. Read the r value in the panel. Is the correlation positive or negative? What does that mean in words?
  3. Check Show stress line. Notice that stress peaks on the same day sleep is lowest. Read the confounder alert.
  4. Choose Wed in the Day menu and drag the gut slider from 7 down to 2. Watch how much r changes because of one day.
  5. Press Clear all and enter a week of your own (real or imaginary). The sim needs at least 3 logged days with some variety before it can compute r.
  6. Press Load sample data to return to Sam's week.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Evaluate. The learner will interpret the correlation between sleep and gut symptoms in a one-week diary and judge the limits of that personal data, including small sample size, confounders such as stress, and the possibility that the effect runs in the reverse direction.

  2. Explore (7 minutes). In pairs, students run steps 1 to 3 of How to Use and write one sentence describing the sleep-gut pattern in Sam's sample week.
  3. Stress-test the pattern (7 minutes). Students run step 4, then try to make r close to zero by changing as few days as possible. Record how many days they changed.
  4. Discuss (6 minutes). Name three explanations for the pattern other than "short sleep causes gut symptoms" (for example, stress as a confounder, gut pain waking Sam up, or expectations shaping his ratings).
  5. Design (5 minutes). Each pair writes a better four-week plan for testing whether sleep matters for Sam's gut, using the "What this model leaves out" box in Chapter 18.

Assessment questions:

  1. In Sam's sample week, r for sleep vs gut symptoms is strongly negative. Explain what that means in plain words.
  2. Why does the sim show a confounder alert, and what would you need to know to rule stress out?
  3. Changing one day can change r a lot. What does that tell you about one week of data?
  4. Give one reason a correlation in a personal diary might run in the opposite direction from what you expect.

docs.title: Conversation Practice
docs.text: Run the Conversation Practice MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Knowing the facts about a gut condition is one skill. Saying them out loud, kindly, to someone who loves you and is wrong, is another. This MicroSim lets you practice that second skill.

There are four short scenarios, all with fictional characters from the textbook:

  • Aunt at dinner: Riya's aunt tells her to "eat more ghee and stop worrying" about her Crohn's disease.
  • Teacher and the restroom: a teacher asks Riya to stay seated during a quiz.
  • Friend asks about missed school: a friend wonders if Riya is "just skipping."
  • Coach before a race: Sam's coach says his IBS is "just nerves."

Each scenario has two turns. You pick one of three replies. The other person's next line depends on what you chose (the conversation branches), and then you pick again. After each choice, a feedback card says whether the reply is likely to land well, mixed (it depends on the moment), or likely to backfire, and explains why. The feedback is a teaching judgment based on the strategies in Chapter 19, not a score. Nothing you choose is saved or sent.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose a scenario from the menu. Read the setting and what the other person says.
  2. Read replies A, B, and C. Before choosing, predict how each might land.
  3. Press Choose A, Choose B, or Choose C and read the feedback card.
  4. Press Next to see how the other person responds to your choice, then choose your second reply.
  5. Press Restart and try a different first reply. Notice how the other person's second line changes.
  6. Try all four scenarios. Then write your own best reply in your own words.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Apply. The learner will use supportive, accurate communication strategies (acknowledge the care behind a comment, give one clear fact, offer a helpful role, set calm boundaries, and bring in backup) to respond to mistaken or stigmatizing comments about gut and mental health, and explain why a given reply might help or backfire.

docs.title: Hype Meter Sorter
docs.text: Run the Hype Meter Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every chapter of Gut Check grades popular claims with the Hype Meter: Strong (consistent evidence in people), Moderate (some human evidence, or a solid link whose cause is unclear), Preliminary (small, early, short, or mostly animal studies), or Hype (a popular claim the evidence does not support).

This MicroSim puts all of that practice in one place. It deals out 16 claim cards drawn from Chapters 1 to 18, such as "70% of your immune system lives in your gut" and "Implanted vagus nerve stimulation is FDA approved for treatment-resistant depression." You grade each card. Then the sim shows the book's grade, a one-sentence reason based on the studies in that chapter, and whether your grade was a match, too generous (closer to Strong than the evidence supports), or too harsh.

The tally at the bottom counts your matches and your misses in each direction. Good scientists aren't just skeptical. They're calibrated: they believe strong evidence and doubt weak evidence.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the claim on the card. Notice the exact wording. The book grades the claim as stated.
  2. Ask the six questions from the Hype Meter: mouse or human, correlation or cause, how many, how long, who paid, and is something being sold.
  3. Click Strong, Moderate, Preliminary, or Hype in the control area.
  4. Read the book's grade and reason. If you missed, decide which evidence feature you overlooked.
  5. Click Next card. Check Show chapter if you want a hint about where the claim came from.
  6. After all 16 cards, read your summary. Click Start over to reshuffle and try again.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Evaluate. The learner will evaluate popular gut-brain claims by assigning a Hype Meter grade based on the kind and amount of evidence, and will judge whether their own grading leans too generous or too harsh.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (biology, health science, AP Psychology, or a science club)

Duration: 25 to 35 minutes

Activity:

  1. Warm-up (5 minutes). Show one card ("Your gut has more neurons than your brain") and ask students to vote by hand on a grade. Discuss what they would need to know to decide.
  2. Sort solo (10 minutes). Each student sorts all 16 cards without the chapter hint and writes down their final score and their "too generous" and "too harsh" counts.
  3. Pair and argue (8 minutes). Partners pick the two cards they missed most and use the chapter reasons to explain the book's grade to each other.
  4. Whole-class debrief (7 minutes). Collect class totals for "too generous" versus "too harsh." Ask: which way does our class lean, and why might social media push people that way?
  5. Limits (5 minutes). Read the "What this model leaves out" box in Chapter 20 and discuss why real grading is less tidy than four buttons.

Assessment questions:

  1. "The gut holds about 70% of the body's antibody-making plasma cells." Why does this true fact not support the claim that 70% of the immune system is in the gut?
  2. Two cards involve vagus nerve stimulation. Why does one earn Strong and the other Preliminary?
  3. Pick one Preliminary card. Describe a study that could move it up to Moderate.
  4. Explain the difference between being skeptical and being calibrated.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

  4. Drag to pan around the graph
  5. Scroll to zoom in and out

  6. Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections

  7. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.
